segments.voiceover: Welcome to this two thousand twenty five board review on pediatric hematology and oncology, presented by Doctor Wang from the pediatrics division. We'll walk through the highest yield topics for your boards, from leukemia genetics to transfusion medicine and oncologic emergencies.

This slide maps out how pediatric board questions have historically been distributed. The biggest chunk, sixty to sixty five percent, is pediatric hematology-oncology itself, covering diagnosis, treatment, side effects, and genetics of ALL, AML, CML, Hodgkin lymphoma, LCH, JMML, and neuroblastoma. General hematology, things like iron deficiency anemia, thalassemia, aplastic anemia, PNH, Diamond-Blackfan anemia, and neutropenia, makes up another twenty to twenty five percent. Transfusion medicine, including blood product storage, indications, and complications like transfusion associated graft versus host disease and TACO, accounts for eight to ten percent. Immune deficiency disorders such as SCID, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, chronic granulomatous disease, and alloimmune neutropenia make up five to seven percent. Oncologic emergencies and treatment complications, like tumor lysis syndrome, differentiation syndrome, cytokine release syndrome, ICANS, and SIADH, account for about five percent. The remaining small slice covers epidemiology, updated diagnostic criteria, rare diseases, and newer topics like CAR-T and gene therapy. Bottom line for exam strategy: prioritize your study time toward hemato-oncology and general hematology, since together they make up over eighty percent of questions.

keypoints: Hemato-oncology (ALL, AML, lymphoma, neuroblastoma): 60-65%
General hematology (IDA, thalassemia, aplastic anemia, PNH): 20-25%
Transfusion medicine (TA-GVHD, TACO): 8-10%
Immune deficiency (SCID, Wiskott-Aldrich, CGD): 5-7%
Oncologic emergencies (TLS, CRS, ICANS, SIADH): 5%
segments.voiceover: Quick recap of exam weighting. Hemato-oncology dominates at sixty to sixty five percent. General hematology topics like thalassemia and aplastic anemia are next at twenty to twenty five percent. Transfusion medicine, immune deficiency disorders, and oncologic emergencies each make up smaller but still testable slices, so don't neglect them.

Here are five recurring themes to anticipate on this year's exam. First, recent literature and guidelines matter a lot, questions frequently draw on journals like Blood, JAMA Oncology, and the New England Journal of Medicine, along with TPOG treatment protocols, the twenty twenty two ELN risk stratification for AML, CAR-T trial data, and newer agents like blinatumomab and emicizumab. Second, clinical management issues are tested through multi-statement questions asking you to pick the correct or incorrect option, focusing on patient risk assessment, treatment selection, and managing drug toxicity. Third, molecular and genetic issues show up across ALL, AML, CML, and neuroblastoma, where you need to know specific gene abnormalities, like KMT2A rearrangements, ETV6-RUNX1 fusion, DUX4 alterations, and MYCN amplification, and how each affects prognosis. Fourth, risk classification and precision medicine are increasingly emphasized, including MRD-directed therapy, CAR-T eligibility criteria, and targeted agents such as gilteritinib, venetoclax, and tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Fifth, expect questions that highlight how age and special populations change clinical presentation and management, think infant ALL, Down syndrome associated AML, adolescent Hodgkin lymphoma, and high-risk groups like SCID and PNH.

keypoints: Know current literature and guidelines: TPOG, ELN 2022, ASH/EHA updates
Gene fusions and prognosis: KMT2A, ETV6-RUNX1, DUX4, MYCN
MRD-directed risk stratification and precision medicine drugs
Age-specific patterns: infant ALL, Down syndrome AML, adolescent HL
segments.voiceover: Remember these five threads as you study: current guidelines and trial data, clinical judgment questions, gene fusions tied to prognosis, MRD-guided precision medicine, and how age or special populations shift the clinical picture.

This slide is a practical study roadmap rather than pure clinical content, but it's worth internalizing for exam prep. The single most important resource is the TPOG protocol and its recent updates, that's highlighted for a reason. Beyond that, stay current with conference highlights from ASH twenty twenty four, EHA twenty twenty four, EHA twenty twenty five, and the ELN or ICC classification updates. Pay attention to major trial results and any new drug approvals or expanded indications, since these frequently become exam vignettes. The speaker also points to broader learning resources, invited lectures from senior faculty, the society's yearly lecture series, and even accessible resources like hematology education Facebook pages. Finally, make sure you're comfortable with immunotherapy concepts that keep coming up, CAR-T, ICANS, cytokine release syndrome, and bispecific T-cell engagers, plus recent publications from pediatric oncology teams.

keypoints: TPOG protocol and its updates are essential exam material
Track ASH/EHA conference highlights and major trial readouts
Watch for new drug approvals and expanded indications
CAR-T, ICANS, CRS, and bispecific T-cell engagers are high-yield
segments.voiceover: Treat this as your exam prep checklist: master the TPOG protocol, follow major conference updates and trial results, track new drug approvals, and be fluent in CAR-T related toxicities and terminology.

Within pediatric hemato-oncology itself, here's how question topics tend to distribute across diseases. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is by far the most heavily tested single disease, with heavy emphasis on treatment, genetic and molecular analysis, and diagnosis, so this deserves the bulk of your preparation time. Acute myeloid leukemia comes next in frequency. Neuroblastoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, and Langerhans cell histiocytosis show up with questions clustered around treatment and diagnosis rather than deep molecular detail. Across all of these diseases, expect recurring questions on treatment-related complications and molecular risk stratification, since these cross-cutting themes get tested repeatedly regardless of which specific tumor is in the vignette.

keypoints: ALL is the single most tested disease: treatment, genetics, diagnosis
AML is the second most common topic
Neuroblastoma, HL, LCH: emphasis on diagnosis and treatment
Treatment complications and molecular risk are recurring cross-cutting themes
segments.voiceover: If you remember one thing from this slide, it's to prioritize ALL, followed by AML, then round out your prep with neuroblastoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, and LCH, while staying alert for treatment complication and molecular risk questions across all of them.

This chart is a classic board favorite because it visually explains why children with ALL do better than adults. Look at the childhood standard risk group on the left, the majority of that bar is high hyperdiploid and ETV6-RUNX1 fusion disease, both favorable, low-risk genetic subtypes. As you move right across childhood high risk, adolescent and young adult, and finally adult patients, that favorable purple and dark blue block shrinks dramatically, while Philadelphia chromosome positive and Philadelphia-like ALL, shown in orange and peach, expand to dominate the adult bars. Ph-like ALL in particular goes from a sliver in young children to a huge portion of the adult bar, and both Ph and Ph-like carry a worse prognosis and often require tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy. KMT2A-rearranged disease is also enriched in the childhood high-risk group, consistent with its association with infant leukemia. The exam takeaway is simple: age itself is a proxy for genetic risk, older patients are enriched for high-risk genetic lesions, which is a major reason ALL outcomes worsen with increasing age.

keypoints: High hyperdiploid and ETV6-RUNX1 fusion dominate in young children, both favorable
Ph and Ph-like ALL rise sharply with age, both high risk, need TKI therapy
KMT2A-rearranged ALL is enriched in childhood high-risk and infant cases
Age correlates with genetic risk, explaining worse ALL outcomes in adults
segments.voiceover: Key exam point: favorable genetics like high hyperdiploid and ETV6-RUNX1 are enriched in young children, while Philadelphia chromosome and Ph-like ALL become much more common with increasing age, and that shift explains the worsening prognosis seen from childhood to adulthood.

This is a dense but extremely high-yield summary slide for ALL risk stratification, worth memorizing in detail. Start with the NCI clinical criteria, standard risk means age one to under ten years, white count under fifty thousand, and no extramedullary involvement, anything outside that, younger than one, older than ten, higher white count, or extramedullary disease, bumps a patient to high risk. Next, the cancer genome panel groups cytogenetics into three tiers. Low risk includes hyperdiploidy over fifty chromosomes, the ETV6-RUNX1 fusion, trisomies four and ten, and for T-ALL, NOTCH1 or FBXW7 mutations. Intermediate risk includes ZNF384 fusions, DUX4 and ERG deregulated subtypes, the TCF3-PBX1 fusion, and for T-ALL, PTEN inactivation or MLL rearrangement. High risk includes the Philadelphia chromosome and Ph-like disease with BCR-ABL1 fusion, KMT2A rearrangements, intrachromosomal amplification of chromosome twenty one, hypodiploidy under forty four chromosomes, IKZF1 and TP53 mutations, MEF2D fusions, and for T-ALL, early T-cell precursor phenotype. The host genome panel covers pharmacogenomics you'll be tested on directly, TPMT and NUDT15 variants predict thiopurine-induced myelosuppression, CEP72 variants predict vincristine peripheral neuropathy, BMP7 and PROX1 antisense RNA variants are linked to glucocorticoid-induced osteonecrosis, and SLCO1B1, DHFR, and miR-1206 variants predict methotrexate-induced mucositis. Finally, minimal residual disease status drives treatment intensity, negative MRD supports treatment reduction in favorable genotypes, while positive MRD prompts intensified chemotherapy or consideration of cellular therapy.

keypoints: NCI risk: age 1-10 plus WBC under 50k, no extramedullary disease, equals standard risk
Favorable: hyperdiploidy over 50, ETV6-RUNX1; Unfavorable: Ph/Ph-like, KMT2A, hypodiploid under 44, IKZF1, TP53
Pharmacogenomics: TPMT/NUDT15 (myelosuppression), CEP72 (neuropathy), SLCO1B1 (MTX mucositis)
MRD-negative favors de-escalation; MRD-positive favors intensification or cellular therapy
segments.voiceover: For the exam, anchor on four buckets: the NCI standard versus high-risk clinical criteria, the three-tier cytogenetic risk groups, the host pharmacogenomic gene-drug-toxicity pairs, and how MRD status directly changes treatment intensity.

This is a research summary of a landmark twenty twenty four New England Journal trial by Gupta and colleagues, testing blinatumomab, a CD19 by CD3 bispecific T-cell engaging antibody, in newly diagnosed standard-risk B-cell ALL. The trial enrolled fourteen hundred forty children between one and ten years old who had an average or higher risk of relapse, randomizing them to standard chemotherapy alone versus chemotherapy plus two nonsequential cycles of intravenous blinatumomab. At a median follow-up of two and a half years, adding blinatumomab significantly improved disease-free survival, ninety six percent versus eighty seven point nine percent, with the benefit consistent across both average and higher relapse risk subgroups. The trade-off was a higher rate of nonfatal sepsis and catheter-related infections in the blinatumomab arm, fourteen point eight percent versus five point one percent. Important limitations for your exam reasoning, high-risk B-cell ALL patients were excluded from this trial, longer follow-up is still needed to confirm durability, and the optimal number and timing of blinatumomab cycles remains unsettled. The takeaway: in standard-risk B-cell ALL with at least average relapse risk, adding blinatumomab to chemotherapy improves disease-free survival at the cost of more infectious complications.

keypoints: Blinatumomab: CD19 x CD3 bispecific T-cell engaging antibody
Added to chemo in standard-risk B-ALL: 3-year DFS 96.0% vs 87.9%
Trade-off: more nonfatal sepsis/catheter infections, 14.8% vs 5.1%
High-risk B-cell ALL patients were NOT included in this trial
segments.voiceover: Remember this trial as the practice-changing evidence for adding blinatumomab to frontline therapy in standard-risk B-cell ALL, it boosts disease-free survival but raises infection risk, and it only applies to standard-risk disease, not high-risk B-ALL.

This table makes a point that's easy to forget on boards, that a negative day forty-two minimal residual disease result doesn't mean the same thing in every patient. Among patients who were M R D negative at day forty-two, those with favorable genotypes, like hyperdiploid or E T V six colon colon R U N X one, had a cumulative relapse risk of just one point three percent. But patients with intermediate or unfavorable genotypes, including P A X five alt, M E F two D rearranged, E T V six colon colon R U N X one like, T cell ALL, i AMP twenty-one, B C R colon colon A B L one, B C R colon colon A B L one like, and K M T two A rearranged, had a relapse risk of nine point five percent, even though their day forty-two M R D was also negative. That's roughly a seven-fold difference, and it's highly significant. The teaching point is that genetic subtype still matters for risk stratification even after you've cleared M R D, so a negative M R D result in a high-risk genotype should not be treated as reassuring as the same result in a favorable genotype.

keypoints: Day 42 MRD-negative does not equal equal risk across genotypes
Favorable genotype MRD-negative: 1.3% relapse risk
Intermediate or unfavorable genotype MRD-negative: 9.5% relapse risk
Genotype still drives risk stratification even after MRD clearance
segments.voiceover: Even with a negative day forty-two M R D, favorable genotype patients had just one point three percent relapse risk, while intermediate or unfavorable genotype patients, like P A X five alt, K M T two A rearranged, or B C R colon colon A B L one, had nine point five percent. Genotype keeps mattering after M R D clears.

This forest plot looks at how East Asian genetic ancestry associates with the odds of having particular molecular subtypes of ALL, and it's a nice illustration of ancestry-driven biology. On the left, in red, are subtypes that are significantly less common with East Asian ancestry, B C R colon colon A B L one like ALL has an odds ratio of zero point three eight, C R L F two rearranged is zero point four one, and T cell ALL is also zero point four one, all with odds ratios below one, meaning East Asian ancestry is protective against these higher-risk subtypes. On the right, in blue, are subtypes significantly enriched in East Asian ancestry, P A X five alt has an odds ratio of one point seven seven, T C F three colon colon P B X one is one point nine eight, D U X four is two point eight four, and Z N F three eight four is three point nine one, all significant with p-values under point zero five. So East Asian patients are more likely to have these particular favorable-to-intermediate rearrangements, and less likely to have B C R colon colon A B L one like or T cell disease. This kind of ancestry data helps explain some of the population differences seen in ALL outcomes and subtype distribution.

keypoints: East Asian ancestry: lower odds of BCR::ABL1-like, CRLF2, and T-ALL
East Asian ancestry: higher odds of PAX5alt, TCF3::PBX1, DUX4, and ZNF384
Odds ratios range from 0.38 for BCR::ABL1-like to 3.91 for ZNF384
Ancestry helps explain population-level differences in ALL subtype distribution
segments.voiceover: East Asian genetic ancestry is associated with lower odds of B C R colon colon A B L one like, C R L F two, and T cell ALL, but higher odds of P A X five alt, T C F three colon colon P B X one, D U X four, and Z N F three eight four, with Z N F three eight four showing nearly a four-fold increased odds.

D U X four rearranged ALL has a distinctive and somewhat paradoxical M R D pattern that's worth knowing cold for boards. Early on, at days eight and fifteen, these patients tend to show poor M R D clearance, and the proposed explanation is relative resistance to asparaginase during that early phase of therapy. But by day forty-two, the picture flips, and D U X four rearranged ALL shows excellent M R D clearance, likely because these leukemic cells are actually quite sensitive to six-mercaptopurine, ara-C, and cyclophosphamide, the drugs that come later in consolidation. The bar chart on the right compares the proportion of M R D-positive cases across timepoints for E T V six colon colon R U N X one, hyperdiploidy greater than fifty, and D U X four rearranged, and you can see the D U X four bars behave differently from the other favorable subtypes, starting high and dropping sharply. The key takeaway is, don't panic and don't escalate therapy just because a D U X four rearranged patient has sluggish early M R D, because by day forty-two, the disease usually clears nicely, and overall this subtype carries a favorable prognosis.

keypoints: DUX4-rearranged ALL: poor day 8 and day 15 MRD clearance
Early poor clearance likely reflects asparaginase resistance
Excellent day 42 MRD, reflecting sensitivity to 6MP, ara-C, cyclophosphamide
Overall prognosis for DUX4-rearranged ALL is favorable despite the early lag
segments.voiceover: D U X four rearranged ALL shows poor early M R D at days eight and fifteen, likely from asparaginase resistance, but then excellent day forty-two M R D thanks to sensitivity to six M P, ara-C, and cyclophosphamide. Don't let the slow early clearance mislead you, the overall prognosis is favorable.

Z N F three eight four rearranged ALL has an immunophenotype that can trip up boards questions because it can masquerade as something else. These blasts characteristically show low expression of C D ten, which is unusual since most B lineage ALL is C D ten positive, and they show high expression of the myeloid markers C D thirteen and C D thirty-three. That aberrant myeloid marker expression is a classic pitfall, it can make the leukemia look like it might be mixed phenotype or even myeloid at first glance, so recognizing this pattern in the context of a B lineage ALL should raise Z N F three eight four rearrangement on your differential. In terms of partner genes, E P three hundred is the most common fusion partner at forty-three percent, followed by T C F three at thirty-one percent, with various others making up the rest. Interestingly, the specific fusion E P three hundred colon colon Z N F three eight four is associated with a lower cumulative risk of relapse and significantly better event-free survival compared to Z N F three eight four rearranged ALL with other partner genes, so even within this one rearrangement category, the partner gene carries prognostic weight.

keypoints: ZNF384-rearranged ALL: low CD10, high CD13 and CD33 expression
Aberrant myeloid marker expression can mimic mixed phenotype leukemia
Most common partner gene is EP300 (43%), then TCF3 (31%)
EP300::ZNF384 fusion carries lower relapse risk and better EFS than other partners
segments.voiceover: Remember the immunophenotype, low C D ten with high C D thirteen and C D thirty-three, which can mimic myeloid disease. E P three hundred is the leading partner gene, and E P three hundred colon colon Z N F three eight four specifically predicts a better outcome than other Z N F three eight four partner fusions.

This slide continues the Z N F three eight four discussion with some newer, therapeutically relevant findings that boards may test as an emerging concept. First, there's a concerning signal that treating relapsed or refractory Z N F three eight four rearranged ALL with blinatumomab or C D nineteen C A R T-cell therapy may actually increase the risk of lineage switch, meaning the leukemia can convert from a B lymphoblastic phenotype to a myeloid phenotype under the selective pressure of C D nineteen-directed immunotherapy. This is thought to relate to the underlying biology of these blasts, which, as we just saw, already have some myeloid marker expression at baseline. Mechanistically, Z N F three eight four rearranged blasts show overexpression of F L T three and upregulation of the J A K-S T A T signaling pathway, which gives a rationale for targeted therapy. Encouragingly, gilteritinib, an F L T three inhibitor already approved in A M L, has shown significant antileukemic efficacy in patient-derived xenograft models of Z N F three eight four rearranged ALL. So the emerging clinical picture is, be cautious about C D nineteen-directed immunotherapy triggering lineage switch in this subtype, and watch for F L T three inhibitors as a potential future targeted option.

keypoints: Blinatumomab or CD19 CAR T-cell therapy may increase lineage switch risk
ZNF384-rearranged blasts overexpress FLT3 and activate JAK-STAT signaling
Gilteritinib, an FLT3 inhibitor, shows efficacy in PDX models
Consider lineage switch risk before choosing CD19-directed immunotherapy
segments.voiceover: CD nineteen-directed therapies like blinatumomab or CAR T can trigger lineage switch in Z N F three eight four rearranged ALL. These blasts overexpress F L T three and activate J A K-S T A T signaling, and the F L T three inhibitor gilteritinib shows promise as a targeted approach in preclinical models.

P A X five alt rearranged ALL is another one of the newer WHO-recognized molecular subtypes, and this slide gives you two testable facts. First, the demographics, these patients tend to present at an older age compared to typical childhood ALL, with a median presenting age of fifteen point four years, so this is a subtype you're more likely to see in adolescents and young adults rather than in toddlers. Second, the outcomes data, which actually looks quite good and differs a bit depending on which cooperative group you look at. In the Children's Oncology Group trial A A L L zero two three two, the five-year event-free survival was seventy-one point five percent plus or minus seven percent. In the St. Jude Total sixteen study, the five-year event-free survival was notably higher, at eighty-two point seven percent. The gap between these two numbers is worth noting, it may reflect differences in treatment intensity, risk stratification, or patient population between the two protocols, but the overall message for boards is that P A X five alt is generally considered a favorable to intermediate risk subtype, distinct from the true P A X five P eight zero R point mutation subtype, which behaves differently.

keypoints: PAX5alt-rearranged ALL presents at an older median age, 15.4 years
COG AALL0232: 5-year EFS 71.5% plus or minus 7.0%
St. Jude Total 16: 5-year EFS 82.7%
Generally a favorable to intermediate risk subtype
segments.voiceover: PAX5alt-rearranged ALL presents later, at a median age of fifteen point four years, and carries a generally favorable outcome, with five-year event-free survival around seventy-one to eighty-three percent depending on the cooperative group protocol.

T C F three colon colon P B X one ALL, which older literature calls E two A colon colon P B X one, results from the translocation t one, nineteen, q two three, p thirteen, and it's a classic, well-established fusion that's been on boards for years. Historically, this subtype was associated with a poorer prognosis compared to standard risk ALL, and in some cohorts it carried an increased risk of C N S relapse, so clinicians developed a habit of treating it more aggressively, including extended pulses of vincristine and dexamethasone during maintenance therapy. But this slide highlights a more recent and practically important finding from the Chinese Children's Cancer Group protocol, C C C G ALL twenty fifteen, which found that extended vincristine and dexamethasone pulse therapy is not actually necessary for children with T C F three colon colon P B X one positive ALL. This is a meaningful shift, because with modern risk-adapted, M R D-guided therapy, this subtype no longer requires the extra treatment intensity it once did, meaning less toxicity exposure for patients without sacrificing outcomes. This is exactly the kind of practice-changing update that boards like to test.

keypoints: Historically linked to poorer prognosis and higher CNS relapse risk
CCCG-ALL-2015: extended vincristine/dexamethasone pulses are not necessary
Reflects a shift toward less treatment intensity with modern risk-adapted therapy
segments.voiceover: T C F three colon colon P B X one, from t one nineteen q two three p thirteen, was historically higher risk with more C N S relapse, but the C C C G ALL twenty fifteen trial showed extended vincristine and dexamethasone pulses are no longer necessary, reflecting modern de-escalation of therapy.

K M T two A rearranged ALL, formerly known as M L L rearranged, is one of the highest-risk subtypes in pediatric ALL, and this slide focuses specifically on the non-infant population, since infant K M T two A ALL is generally discussed separately. Among non-infant cases, t four, eleven, q twenty-one, q twenty-three, producing the K M T two A colon colon A F F one fusion, had the worst event-free survival of any K M T two A partner, so if you see this specific translocation on boards, flag it as particularly high risk. As with most high-risk ALL subtypes, minimal residual disease at the end of induction was the single most important prognostic factor, and this held true both for K M T two A colon colon A F F one ALL and for K M T two A rearranged T-cell ALL, reinforcing that M R D response trumps genotype alone when predicting outcome. Finally, and this is a somewhat counterintuitive but important point, allogeneic stem cell transplant failed to improve outcomes for K M T two A colon colon A F F one ALL in this data, which challenges the older assumption that transplant automatically benefits every high-risk genetic subtype, and pushes the field toward finding better targeted approaches, like menin inhibitors, rather than relying on transplant alone.

keypoints: Non-infant t(4;11)(q21;q23), KMT2A::AFF1, has the worst EFS among KMT2A subtypes
End-of-induction MRD is the strongest prognostic factor in KMT2A::AFF1 and KMT2A-rearranged T-ALL
Allogeneic transplant did not improve outcomes in KMT2A::AFF1 ALL
Highlights the need for targeted approaches beyond transplant in this high-risk subtype
segments.voiceover: Non-infant K M T two A colon colon A F F one ALL, from t four eleven, carries the worst outcomes among K M T two A subtypes, end-of-induction M R D is the key prognostic factor, and notably, allogeneic transplant failed to improve outcomes in this group.

This slide covers KMT2A rearranged ALL, one of the highest risk genetic subtypes, especially in infants. The top panel shows a modern treatment backbone that adds blinatumomab early, right after induction, before moving into Protocol IB, then MARMA and OCTADAD consolidation blocks, and finally maintenance. Medium risk patients who still have measurable residual disease of five times ten to the minus four or higher before OCTADAD, and all high risk patients, are triaged to stem cell transplant. The bottom panels show why this matters. Compared with the older Interfant zero six regimen, the current blinatumomab containing study nearly doubles two year disease free survival, eighty one point six percent versus forty nine point four percent, and substantially improves two year overall survival, ninety three point three percent versus sixty five point eight percent. For boards, remember that incorporating blinatumomab into infant KMT2A rearranged ALL therapy is a major recent practice change with strong survival benefit, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in twenty twenty three.

keypoints: Blinatumomab added early in KMT2A rearranged ALL therapy
Transplant reserved for high risk and MRD positive medium risk patients
Two year disease free survival roughly doubled versus Interfant zero six
Two year overall survival improved from about sixty six to ninety three percent
segments.voiceover: Key points to remember. Blinatumomab is now added early in the treatment course for KMT2A rearranged ALL. Transplant is reserved for high risk patients and for medium risk patients who remain MRD positive before OCTADAD. This approach roughly doubled two year disease free survival compared with Interfant zero six, and pushed two year overall survival up to about ninety three percent.

Now we turn to MEF2D rearranged ALL, a distinct B cell precursor subtype. It shows a striking female predominance of sixty six percent and tends to occur in older children, with a median age of ten point seven years, and nearly sixty percent of patients being ten years or older. On immunophenotype, these blasts frequently express cytoplasmic mu chain in about eighty two percent of cases, CD5 in fifty six percent, and are often CD10 negative, seen in about thirty five percent, which can be a diagnostic clue since most B ALL is CD10 positive. The fusion partner matters prognostically. MEF2D BCL9 is the most common partner, found in fifty four percent of cases, but it carries a worse event free survival of only about sixty five percent. In contrast, MEF2D HNRNPUL1, seen in thirty two percent, has a much better outcome, with event free survival around ninety four percent. Other rarer partners make up the remaining fourteen percent. Overall, with modern therapy, MRD negative remission is achieved in ninety three percent of patients, and five year event free survival is seventy four percent.

keypoints: Female predominance, sixty six percent, and older median age of ten point seven years
Frequent cytoplasmic mu, CD5 positive, and CD10 negative immunophenotype
MEF2D BCL9 partner has worse outcome than MEF2D HNRNPUL1
Overall five year event free survival about seventy four percent
segments.voiceover: Key points. MEF2D rearranged ALL favors older girls, with a CD10 negative, CD5 positive immunophenotype. The fusion partner drives prognosis, MEF2D BCL9 does worse, while MEF2D HNRNPUL1 does much better. Overall five year event free survival is around seventy four percent.

Here is a board style test question on cytogenetic and molecular abnormalities in childhood ALL. It asks which statements are correct. Statement one says Ph-like associated molecular changes include IGH-CRLF2 rearrangement, ABL class fusions, JAK2 rearrangement, and EPOR rearrangement, and that is correct, these are the classic Ph-like signaling lesions. Statement two says the ETV6 RUNX1 fusion gene is associated with excellent prognosis, and that is also correct, it's one of the most favorable genetic subtypes in pediatric ALL. Statement three says iAMP21 carries a worse prognosis and requires more intensive chemotherapy, which is correct as well, intrachromosomal amplification of chromosome 21 is a recognized high risk feature. Statement four claims that translocations involving DUX4, MEF2D, and ZNF384 are common in adolescents and all carry poor prognosis. This is false, these three subtypes are biologically distinct and do not uniformly carry poor prognosis, DUX4 rearranged ALL in particular tends to have a favorable outcome. So the correct combination is statements one, two, and three, which corresponds to answer B.

keypoints: Ph-like ALL molecular lesions include IGH-CRLF2, ABL class fusions, JAK2 and EPOR rearrangements
ETV6 RUNX1 fusion confers excellent prognosis
iAMP21 confers worse prognosis and needs intensified chemotherapy
DUX4, MEF2D, and ZNF384 rearrangements do not all carry poor prognosis, statement four is false
Correct answer is B, statements one plus two plus three
segments.voiceover: Key points for this question. Ph-like ALL includes IGH-CRLF2, ABL class fusions, JAK2, and EPOR rearrangements. ETV6 RUNX1 is a favorable fusion. iAMP21 is high risk and needs intensified therapy. But DUX4, MEF2D, and ZNF384 rearrangements are not uniformly poor prognosis, so statement four is wrong, making the correct answer B, statements one, two, and three.

This is Appendix I, the treatment schema of TPOG ALL twenty twenty one for B cell ALL. It lays out two parallel tracks, standard risk on top and high risk or very high risk on the bottom, defined by MRD checkpoints at day fifteen, day forty two, and a later MRD3 assessment. Standard risk patients move through Induction I and II A, then either high dose methotrexate and mercaptopurine cycles or, if MRD at day fifteen is one percent or higher, an extra EI star block before consolidation, followed by re-induction and cyclical maintenance chemotherapy. High risk and very high risk patients get more intensive Induction II B or C, extra intensification blocks, and critically, two cycles of blinatumomab, labeled Blincyto I and II, built into consolidation. After blinatumomab, MRD is reassessed, if positive, the patient proceeds to HSCT or CAR T cell therapy, if negative, they continue with re-induction and maintenance. The timeline at the bottom shows the overall structure, remission and early intensification for the first nine weeks, consolidation over the next eight weeks, continuation and reinduction from week one to twenty, and then long term continuation therapy out to week one twenty, roughly two and a half years total.

keypoints: Two parallel tracks, standard risk versus high risk and very high risk, driven by MRD
MRD checked at day fifteen, day forty two, and MRD3
High risk and very high risk patients receive two cycles of blinatumomab in consolidation
MRD positive after blinatumomab leads to HSCT or CAR T cell therapy
Total therapy duration extends to about week one twenty
segments.voiceover: Key points on this TPOG ALL twenty twenty one B-ALL schema. Risk group and MRD response, checked at day fifteen, day forty two, and MRD3, drive the treatment path. High risk and very high risk patients get blinatumomab built into consolidation. If MRD stays positive afterward, the patient moves to transplant or CAR T cell therapy. Total treatment runs out to about week one twenty.

This is Appendix II, the treatment schema of TPOG ALL twenty twenty one for T cell ALL. It splits patients into early T cell precursor, or ETP, and non ETP subtypes, each following a similar backbone. Both start with Induction I and Induction II C over the first several weeks, followed by an intensification block, EI plus for most patients, or V-EI specifically for ETP cases. MRD is checked at day fifteen, day forty two, and day seventy. Based on that MRD result, patients enter a menu of treatment options, footnoted at the bottom, before a decision point, if MRD remains positive, the patient goes to transplant, if negative, they continue with high dose methotrexate and mercaptopurine cycles, re-induction I and II, and then long term continuation therapy. Note that ETP ALL requires MRD of zero point one percent or higher after EI plus or V-EI to trigger the intensified pathway, while non ETP uses a slightly different threshold combining MRD2 and the post EI plus MRD value. The overall timeline mirrors the B-ALL schema, extending out to week one twenty.

keypoints: T-ALL is split into ETP and non-ETP arms with similar overall backbone
MRD checkpoints at day fifteen, day forty two, and day seventy guide therapy
ETP patients get V-EI intensification, non-ETP get EI plus
Persistent MRD positivity after intensification leads to HSCT
Different MRD thresholds define high risk for ETP versus non-ETP
segments.voiceover: Key points for T-ALL treatment under TPOG twenty twenty one. ETP and non ETP subtypes follow a similar induction and intensification backbone, but ETP uses V-EI while non ETP uses EI plus. MRD is checked at day fifteen, forty two, and seventy, and persistent MRD positivity after intensification triggers transplant. The MRD thresholds defining high risk differ slightly between ETP and non ETP.

This slide details the MRD based risk stratification algorithm used in the TPOG B-ALL protocol. On the left, starting from a provisional high risk assignment, patients get Induction I, then MRD1 is checked. If MRD1 is less than five percent, they proceed to the somewhat less intensive Induction II B, if five percent or higher, they get the more intensive Induction II C. After that block, MRD2 is checked, less than one percent keeps the patient in the high risk group and they get standard EI plus intensification, while one percent or higher escalates them to very high risk with augmented EI plus therapy. On the right, we zoom into what happens when MRD2 is positive. Any detectable MRD2 triggers blinatumomab, recommended per protocol, followed by an MRD3 check. Depending on whether MRD2 was zero point zero one to zero point nine nine percent versus one percent or higher, and what MRD3 shows afterward, patients are directed toward continuation as high risk, optional reintensification, escalation to very high risk with one to three cycles of reintensification, or ultimately HSCT or CAR T therapy if MRD remains at or above zero point zero one percent and is not decreasing. The footnotes flag important exceptions, hyperdiploid B-ALL with MRD2 one percent or higher can have MRD3 checked immediately after consolidation, before blinatumomab, to finalize risk classification, and B-ALL with persistent MRD positivity after week seven of continuation can still access blinatumomab through the national insurance program if it hasn't been used yet.

keypoints: MRD1 threshold of five percent determines Induction II-B versus II-C
MRD2 threshold of one percent separates high risk from very high risk
Any positive MRD2 triggers blinatumomab, followed by MRD3 reassessment
Persistent or rising MRD after blinatumomab leads to reintensification or HSCT and CAR T
Hyperdiploid B-ALL has a special exception allowing earlier MRD3 checking
segments.voiceover: Key points on this MRD algorithm. MRD1 at five percent separates Induction II-B from II-C. MRD2 at one percent separates high risk from very high risk. Any positive MRD2 triggers blinatumomab followed by MRD3 reassessment, and persistent or rising MRD after that leads to reintensification or ultimately transplant or CAR T therapy. Hyperdiploid B-ALL has a special earlier MRD3 checkpoint.

This flow chart details induction, early intensification, consolidation, and reintensification specifically for T cell ALL, again split into non ETP on the left and ETP on the right. Both subtypes get Induction I, MRD1 is checked but any result proceeds to Induction II C, since T-ALL is uniformly treated more intensively at this stage. After Induction II C, MRD2 is checked. If it's less than zero point zero one percent, patients get standard EI plus and are simply treated as high risk going forward. If MRD2 is zero point zero one percent or higher, non ETP patients still get EI plus, but ETP patients specifically move to V-EI instead. All patients with MRD2 at or above zero point zero one percent then proceed to an MRD3 checkpoint. Less than zero point zero one percent allows consolidation as high risk. Zero point zero one to zero point zero nine percent triggers a menu of Tx options, shown in the yellow box on the right, ETP patients get V-EI, while non ETP patients can receive dasatinib if drug sensitivity is identified, a high dose Ara-C based reintensification regimen, or nelarabine based therapy. Finally, MRD3 of zero point one percent or higher after Tx options leads straight to HSCT.

keypoints: Both non-ETP and ETP T-ALL get Induction I then Induction II C
MRD2 at zero point zero one percent threshold determines EI plus versus V-EI for ETP
MRD3 stratifies into consolidation as high risk, Tx options, or transplant pathway
Tx options include dasatinib, high dose Ara-C based regimen, or nelarabine for non-ETP
MRD3 at zero point one percent or higher leads to HSCT
segments.voiceover: Key points on this T-ALL induction and intensification flow chart. Both ETP and non ETP get Induction I and Induction II C. MRD2 at zero point zero one percent determines whether ETP patients switch to V-EI. MRD3 then stratifies patients into consolidation as high risk, a menu of Tx options like dasatinib or nelarabine, or straight to HSCT if MRD3 is zero point one percent or higher.

This slide summarizes the diagnostic criteria for Early T-cell Precursor, or ETP, ALL, a biologically distinct and historically high risk subtype of T-ALL. All four criteria must be met simultaneously. Criteria one requires an unequivocal diagnosis of T-ALL, meaning CD3 positive, either surface or cytoplasmic, CD7 positive, and myeloperoxidase negative, which rules out mixed phenotype or myeloid disease. Criteria two requires the blasts to be CD1a negative and CD8 negative, reflecting an immature, pre cortical stage of T cell development. Criteria three requires dim CD5 expression, defined as a mean fluorescence intensity at least ten fold lower than normal T lymphocytes in the same sample, or fewer than seventy five percent of blasts being CD5 positive. Finally, criteria four requires expression of stem cell associated antigens, such as CD34, CD133, CD117, or HLA-DR, and or myeloid associated antigens, such as CD13, CD33, CD15, or CD11b, and positivity for just one of these markers is enough to satisfy this criterion. Together, this immunophenotype reflects an early, multipotent thymocyte that has not committed to full T lineage differentiation, which is why ETP ALL behaves differently and is risk stratified separately, as we saw in the preceding treatment algorithms.

keypoints: All four criteria must be met for ETP ALL diagnosis
Unequivocal T-ALL, CD3 positive, CD7 positive, myeloperoxidase negative
CD1a negative and CD8 negative
Dim CD5, MFI at least ten fold lower than normal T cells, or under seventy five percent CD5 positive
Stem cell or myeloid associated antigen expression, any one marker is sufficient
segments.voiceover: Key points for ETP ALL diagnosis. All four criteria must be met together. First, unequivocal T-ALL with CD3 positive, CD7 positive, and MPO negative. Second, CD1a negative and CD8 negative. Third, dim CD5 expression. Fourth, expression of at least one stem cell or myeloid associated antigen. This immature immunophenotype is why ETP ALL is risk stratified separately.

This slide walks through the 2025 revision notes for early T precursor, or ETP, and near ETP acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The background is that outcomes for ETP ALL remained poor, and patients with a poor response often had a high MRD1 or even outright induction failure. Based on that experience, the protocol was revised in several ways around venetoclax. Venetoclax is now started earlier, during induction itself, rather than waiting. The duration of the venetoclax plus early intensification combination, abbreviated V-E-I, has been shortened. Reinduction with venetoclax, phases one and two, is now used more often. And the intensity of chemotherapy across the different phases has been adjusted accordingly to balance toxicity and efficacy. Note also that venetoclax currently requires self-payment in Taiwan, but the childhood cancer foundation now provides full subsidy. The second half of the slide defines the near ETP immunophenotype. Classic ETP still requires all four criteria to be met. Near ETP means criteria one, two, and four are satisfied, but criterion three is not, for example when CD5 is expressed at higher levels than expected. The table spells out those criteria: criterion one is an unequivocal T-ALL diagnosis with CD3 positive, CD7 positive, and myeloperoxidase negative; criterion two is CD1a negative and CD8 negative; and criterion four is expression of stem cell associated antigens like CD34, CD133, CD117, or HLA-D-R, or myeloid associated antigens like CD13, CD33, CD15, or CD11b, where just one positive marker is enough.

keypoints: ETP ALL has poor outcomes, prompting a 2025 venetoclax protocol revision
Venetoclax started earlier in induction, shorter V-E-I duration, more reinduction use
Near ETP meets criteria one, two, and four but not three, such as higher CD5
ETP diagnosis requires CD3 positive, CD7 positive, MPO negative, plus CD1a and CD8 negative
Venetoclax needs self-payment but is now fully subsidized by the childhood cancer foundation
segments.voiceover: Key points here. ETP ALL has poor outcomes, which drove this 2025 venetoclax revision. Venetoclax now starts earlier in induction, with a shorter V-E-I course and more reinduction use. Near ETP is defined as meeting criteria one, two, and four, but not criterion three, such as higher CD5 expression. Classic ETP requires CD3 positive, CD7 positive, myeloperoxidase negative, plus CD1a and CD8 negative. And venetoclax, though self-pay, is now fully subsidized by the childhood cancer foundation.

This is the flow chart for the TPOG-ALL-2021 protocol as revised for ETP and near ETP patients. Treatment begins with ETP induction, followed by an MRD check at MRD1, and induction continues regardless of that result. Then comes a second phase of ETP induction, followed by MRD2. After that, all patients move into venetoclax plus early intensification, the V-E-I phase, followed by MRD3. This MRD3 result is the key branch point. If MRD3 is less than 0.01 percent, the patient proceeds directly to high risk consolidation and then continuation therapy. If MRD3 is between 0.01 and 0.1 percent, the patient also goes to high risk consolidation, but then has an additional MRD check, MRD4, after that consolidation; if MRD4 is now less than 0.01 percent they proceed to continuation, but if it remains at or above 0.01 percent they move to treatment options. If MRD3 is 0.1 percent or higher, the patient goes straight to treatment options. Those treatment options include venetoclax combined with hyper-CVAD, nelarabine based therapy, or high dose ara-C based regimens such as reintensification regimen A. Patients who go down the treatment options pathway ultimately proceed to hematopoietic stem cell transplant. The footnote clarifies that MRD1 and MRD2 are used to judge the efficacy of ETP induction, while MRD3 is specifically obtained for ETP patients whose MRD2 was 0.01 percent or higher.

keypoints: Sequence: ETP induction, MRD1, ETP induction continued, MRD2, then V-E-I, then MRD3
MRD3 under 0.01 percent goes straight to consolidation and continuation
MRD3 between 0.01 and 0.1 percent needs an extra MRD4 check after consolidation
MRD3 at or above 0.1 percent, or a positive MRD4, leads to treatment options and eventual HSCT
Treatment options include venetoclax-hyper-CVAD, nelarabine-based therapy, or high-dose ara-C regimens
segments.voiceover: To summarize the flow. Patients go through ETP induction with MRD1, more induction with MRD2, then venetoclax plus early intensification leading to MRD3, which is the major decision point. MRD3 under 0.01 percent means straight to consolidation and continuation. Between 0.01 and 0.1 percent triggers an extra MRD4 check after consolidation. And MRD3 at 0.1 percent or higher, or a persistently positive MRD4, routes the patient to salvage treatment options like venetoclax hyper-CVAD, nelarabine, or high-dose ara-C, ultimately heading toward transplant.

This table outlines the risk classification for the TPOG-Infant ALL-2022 protocol, which is specifically for infants with acute lymphoblastic leukemia, stratified by KMT2A gene status. First, if KMT2A is germline, meaning no rearrangement, the patient is low risk and is treated on the standard TPOG-ALL-2021 protocol, provisionally as high risk. Second, if KMT2A is rearranged but there are no high risk clinical features, the patient is intermediate risk. Within that group, if MRD is less than 0.01 percent after consolidation, at the time point called TP4, the patient stays on the intermediate risk infant protocol. If MRD remains higher than that, the patient is escalated to intermediate risk plus either transplant or CAR-T cell therapy. Third, if KMT2A is rearranged and high risk clinical features are present, meaning age less than six months, or a white blood cell count of 300,000 per cubic millimeter or higher, the patient is classified as high risk. Again, if MRD is less than 0.01 percent after consolidation at TP4, they follow the high risk infant protocol alone, but if MRD remains elevated, they escalate to high risk plus transplant or CAR-T. So the take home is that infant ALL risk stratification depends on both the genetic driver, KMT2A rearrangement status, clinical high risk features like young age and hyperleukocytosis, and early treatment response measured by MRD.

keypoints: KMT2A germline infant ALL is low risk, treated on standard TPOG-ALL-2021 protocol
KMT2A rearranged without high-risk features is intermediate risk
High-risk features are age under six months or WBC 300,000 per mm3 or higher
MRD under 0.01 percent after consolidation, TP4, keeps patients on IR or HR protocol alone
Persistent MRD at TP4 escalates either group to HSCT or CAR-T therapy
segments.voiceover: Quick recap. KMT2A germline infants are low risk and follow the standard ALL protocol. KMT2A rearranged infants without high-risk features are intermediate risk, while age under six months or WBC over 300,000 defines high risk. In both intermediate and high risk groups, MRD less than 0.01 percent after consolidation at TP4 means staying on that risk-adapted protocol, but persistent MRD escalates the patient to transplant or CAR-T therapy.

This slide details the treatment schema for intermediate and high risk infant ALL under the TPOG-Infant ALL-2022 protocol. Treatment starts with four weeks of induction containing venetoclax, followed by a fifteen day course of blinatumomab, the first of two planned blinatumomab courses. Then comes ten weeks of early consolidation, after which MRD is checked at time point TP4. That result determines whether the patient is intermediate risk or high risk going forward, but both groups then receive a second fifteen day course of blinatumomab, followed by three weeks of venetoclax reinduction and six weeks of late consolidation. From there, the two risk groups diverge slightly in maintenance: intermediate risk patients receive maintenance A for four weeks times five cycles, while high risk patients instead receive a venetoclax containing maintenance for the same duration; both groups then converge onto maintenance B and maintenance C. Notably, if MRD is positive at the TP4 branch point, the patient is diverted to a three week venetoclax reinduction followed by options for second line therapy, with a further MRD check determining whether the patient proceeds to CAR-T, if MRD is positive, or HSCT, if MRD is negative. The bottom of the slide reinforces the HSCT indications: persistent MRD of 0.01 percent or higher after early consolidation at TP4 warrants transplant after reinduction, and any MRD recurrence during maintenance also warrants transplant once a negative MRD status is re-achieved with salvage therapy. The timeline at the bottom shows MRD is checked at six time points, TP1 through TP6, then every three to four months thereafter.

keypoints: Induction-Ve for four weeks, then blinatumomab I for fifteen days, then early consolidation
MRD at TP4 splits patients into IR or HR pathways, both get blinatumomab II
Positive MRD at the TP4 branch triggers reinduction, second-line options, then CAR-T or HSCT by MRD result
HSCT is indicated for persistent MRD 0.01 percent or higher after early consolidation
HSCT is also indicated for any MRD recurrence during maintenance, after achieving MRD negativity with salvage
segments.voiceover: In summary, infants get induction with venetoclax, blinatumomab course one, then early consolidation, with MRD checked at TP4 to assign intermediate or high risk, and both groups then receive a second blinatumomab course. If that MRD branch is positive instead, patients get reinduction and second line options, heading to CAR-T if MRD stays positive or HSCT if it clears. Overall, transplant is indicated for persistent MRD of 0.01 percent or more after early consolidation, or for any MRD recurrence during maintenance once salvage therapy restores MRD negativity.

This is a quick self test on stem cell transplant indications under current TPOG-ALL therapy. The question asks which of four clinical scenarios should prompt a recommendation for hematopoietic stem cell transplant. Scenario one is a high risk B-ALL patient whose MRD had turned negative but then became positive again, meaning MRD recurrence. Scenario two is a high risk B-ALL patient who completed two courses of blinatumomab but still has positive MRD. Scenario three is a T-ALL patient who completed early intensification plus venetoclax therapy but still has positive MRD. Scenario four is a KMT2A rearranged infant ALL patient who completed venetoclax containing and blinatumomab therapy with positive MRD, then received second line therapy and became MRD negative. Working through the logic from the prior slides: scenario one clearly qualifies, since MRD recurrence after negativity is a standard transplant indication. Scenario two qualifies too, since persistent MRD positivity despite maximal blinatumomab therapy in high risk B-ALL is a treatment failure warranting transplant. Scenario three also qualifies, mirroring the ETP pathway where persistent MRD after venetoclax based intensification triggers transplant. Scenario four is the interesting one: even though the patient achieved MRD negativity after second line therapy, the infant protocol schema specifically shows that after second line therapy, an MRD negative result still routes to HSCT rather than continuing chemotherapy alone, because that MRD positivity after first line venetoclax and blinatumomab already signaled high risk disease. So the correct answer combines all four scenarios, which is answer E, one plus two plus three plus four.

keypoints: Scenario one, MRD recurrence after prior negativity, is a classic HSCT indication
Scenario two, persistent MRD positive despite two blinatumomab courses in high-risk B-ALL, warrants HSCT
Scenario three, persistent MRD positive after venetoclax-based intensification in T-ALL, warrants HSCT
Scenario four, infant ALL becoming MRD negative only after second-line therapy, still warrants HSCT
The correct answer is E, all four scenarios call for hematopoietic stem cell transplant
segments.voiceover: To recap this test question. All four scenarios turn out to warrant transplant: MRD recurrence after negativity, persistent MRD despite full blinatumomab therapy in high-risk B-ALL, persistent MRD after venetoclax intensification in T-ALL, and even an infant ALL patient who only achieves MRD negativity after switching to second-line therapy, since that late response still reflects high risk disease. So the correct answer is E, all four combined.

This slide covers the risk stratification section of the TPOG-AML-2021 protocol. Low risk patients receive five courses of chemotherapy and are not eligible for stem cell transplant. Low risk is defined by favorable cytogenetics: inversion 16, t(8;21), NPM1 mutation, or CENPA, combined with MRD less than 0.1 percent after the first induction course. Intermediate risk patients receive six courses of chemotherapy and are also not transplant candidates; this group is essentially defined by exclusion, meaning the absence of any low risk or high risk features. High risk patients are candidates for stem cell transplant, and this category is defined by the presence of any of seven criteria. The first is a long list of specific high risk cytogenetic and molecular lesions, including DEK-NUP214 from t(6;9), KAT6A-CREBBP from t(8;16), monosomy 7, monosomy 5, or 5q deletion, KMT2A-MLLT6 from t(6;11), KMT2A-MLLT10 from t(10;11), inversion 3 at q21q26.2, CBFA2T3-GLIS2 from inversion 16 at p13.3q24.3, NUP98-KDM5A, ETV6-HLXB, NUP98-HOXA9, and NUP98-NSD1. Second is FLT3-ITD combined with either NUP98-NSD1 fusion or WT1 mutation. Third is AML with minimal differentiation or acute erythroid leukemia. Fourth is acute megakaryoblastic leukemia specifically when it carries KMT2A rearrangements, CBFA2T3-GLIS2, or NUP98-KDM5, noting that other megakaryoblastic leukemia subtypes are only intermediate risk. Fifth is treatment related, or secondary, AML. Sixth is refractory anemia with excess blasts and more than 10 percent bone marrow blasts, or AML arising from prior MDS. And seventh is poor response to therapy, defined as MRD 1 percent or higher after induction one, or MRD 0.1 percent or higher after induction two.

keypoints: Low risk: favorable cytogenetics like inv16, t(8;21), NPM1, or CENPA, plus MRD under 0.1 percent after induction I, gets 5 chemo courses only
Intermediate risk is defined by absence of low- or high-risk features, gets 6 chemo courses, no SCT
High risk patients are SCT candidates, defined by any of seven adverse features
High-risk cytogenetics include DEK-NUP214, KAT6A-CREBBP, monosomy 5 or 7, several KMT2A and NUP98 fusions
Poor response also defines high risk: MRD 1 percent or higher after induction I, or 0.1 percent or higher after induction II
segments.voiceover: Bottom line for AML risk groups. Low risk means favorable cytogenetics plus a good early MRD response, treated with five courses and no transplant. Intermediate risk is everyone without low- or high-risk features, getting six courses. High risk, which makes patients transplant candidates, includes a long list of adverse cytogenetic and molecular lesions, FLT3-ITD with NUP98-NSD1 or WT1 mutation, minimally differentiated or erythroid AML, certain megakaryoblastic leukemias, secondary AML, and simply a poor MRD response after induction.

This slide focuses on leukemia in children with Down syndrome, who carry a ten to twenty fold increased risk of leukemia compared to the general population. For ALL in Down syndrome, most patients fall into the standard risk group. However, these children tolerate chemotherapy less well and are more toxic to treatment, so close monitoring is essential. Because of that increased toxicity, dosing is specifically adjusted: high dose methotrexate is reduced from the usual 2.5 grams per meter squared down to 0.5 grams per meter squared, with early leucovorin rescue, during consolidation therapy. And for patients in the high risk or very high risk groups, dexamethasone and or high dose cytarabine doses are also reduced. For AML in Down syndrome, the biology is quite distinct. There's an increased frequency of the M7 subtype, acute megakaryoblastic leukemia, and this is driven by GATA1 mutations. Despite the underlying myeloid malignancy, outcomes are markedly superior compared to non-Down syndrome AML. These patients typically present with a lower initial white blood cell count, no central nervous system involvement, and fewer cytogenetic abnormalities overall. Given both the excellent prognosis and the heightened treatment sensitivity, Down syndrome AML should be treated with less intensive chemotherapy regimens: high dose cytarabine remains part of therapy, but anthracycline dosing and intrathecal therapy are both reduced compared to standard AML protocols.

keypoints: Down syndrome carries a ten to twenty-fold increased leukemia risk versus the general population
Down syndrome ALL is mostly standard risk but more chemotherapy-toxic, so HD-MTX is reduced to 0.5 g per m2
Down syndrome AML has increased M7, acute megakaryoblastic leukemia, driven by GATA1 mutations
Down syndrome AML has markedly better outcomes than non-Down syndrome AML
Down syndrome AML treatment should be less intensive: reduced anthracycline and reduced intrathecal therapy
segments.voiceover: Key takeaways. Down syndrome raises leukemia risk ten to twenty fold. Down syndrome ALL is usually standard risk but more toxicity-prone, so high dose methotrexate is cut down to 0.5 grams per meter squared with leucovorin rescue. Down syndrome AML skews toward M7, acute megakaryoblastic leukemia, driven by GATA1 mutation, and despite being AML it actually carries a much better prognosis than non-Down syndrome AML, which is why treatment intensity, especially anthracycline and intrathecal therapy, is deliberately reduced.

This slide covers juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia, or JMMoL, a rare and aggressive myeloid neoplasm of early childhood that sits in the overlap category of myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative neoplasms, MDS slash MPN. Diagnosis relies on three categories of criteria. Category one lists mandatory clinical and hematologic features, and all of them must be present: a peripheral blood monocyte count greater than 1 times ten to the ninth per liter, blasts in peripheral blood and bone marrow under 20 percent, splenomegaly, and absence of the t(9;22) BCR-ABL fusion gene, which rules out chronic myeloid leukemia. Category two covers molecular diagnostics, and only one of these needs to be present: a somatic mutation in PTPN11, KRAS, or NRAS; a clinical diagnosis of neurofibromatosis type 1 or a germline NF1 mutation; or a germline CBL mutation with loss of heterozygosity of CBL. Category three lists additional supportive hematologic features, and at least two are required only if none of the category two molecular criteria are met; these include monosomy 7 or another clonal cytogenetic abnormality, increased fetal hemoglobin for age, circulating myeloid precursors on the peripheral smear, white blood cell count over 10 times ten to the ninth per liter, granulocyte-macrophage colony stimulating factor hypersensitivity in a colony assay, and hyperphosphorylation of STAT5. Pathogenesis centers on a hyperactive RAS signaling pathway, which makes sense given that PTPN11, KRAS, NRAS, NF1, and CBL are all RAS pathway genes. Prognosis is variable: about one third of patients have aggressive disease with rapid progression, and median survival without transplant is less than one year, though spontaneous resolution can occur in patients with CBL mutations or germline PTPN11 mutations. Treatment is curative only with HSCT; before transplant, asymptomatic patients may simply be observed, or disease burden may be decreased with cytoreductive therapy.

keypoints: JMMoL is a rare aggressive childhood MDS/MPN overlap neoplasm
Diagnosis needs all category 1 clinical features, plus 1 category 2 molecular criterion, or 2 category 3 features if category 2 is negative
Category 2 mutations are PTPN11, KRAS, NRAS, NF1, or germline CBL with loss of heterozygosity
Pathogenesis is hyperactive RAS signaling; median survival without HSCT is under one year
HSCT is the only curative treatment; CBL or germline PTPN11 mutations can allow spontaneous resolution
segments.voiceover: To summarize JMMoL. It is a rare, aggressive childhood MDS-MPN overlap disease. Diagnosis requires all the mandatory clinical features, plus either one molecular hit among PTPN11, KRAS, NRAS, NF1, or germline CBL, or, lacking that, at least two supportive hematologic features. Pathogenesis is driven by hyperactive RAS signaling, prognosis is poor with median survival under a year without transplant, though CBL or germline PTPN11 mutations can spontaneously resolve, and HSCT remains the only curative treatment.

This slide covers targeted therapy for Ph-like ALL, a high-risk subtype that mimics Philadelphia chromosome positive leukemia genetically but lacks the BCR-ABL1 fusion. For patients with CRLF2 rearrangement plus JAK2 or EPOR rearrangement, and who have persistent minimal residual disease, meaning MRD1 greater than or equal to 5 percent or MRD2 greater than or equal to 1 percent, you can apply for compassionate use of ruxolitinib, a JAK inhibitor. The dosing is 50 milligrams per meter squared per dose by mouth twice daily, with a maximum of 200 milligrams per day, given on a schedule of 2 weeks on and 2 weeks off, starting on the day of Early Intensification. For patients with ABL class chimeric fusions, involving genes like ABL1, ABL2, CSF1R, PDGFRA, or PDGFRB, dasatinib is the drug of choice because these fusions create a kinase that responds to tyrosine kinase inhibition similar to BCR-ABL1. Dasatinib is dosed at 80 milligrams per meter squared per day, maximum 140 milligrams, and can be started as soon as the genetic aberration is identified regardless of the MRD level. In practice, prior authorization for dasatinib through national health insurance is often tied to the MRD results.

keypoints: Ph-like ALL with CRLF2 plus JAK2 or EPOR rearrangement and high MRD may qualify for compassionate-use ruxolitinib
Ruxolitinib dosing is 50 mg per m2 twice daily, max 200 mg per day, 2 weeks on 2 weeks off starting at Early Intensification
ABL class fusions such as ABL1, ABL2, CSF1R, PDGFRA, or PDGFRB respond to dasatinib regardless of MRD level
Dasatinib dosing is 80 mg per m2 per day, maximum 140 mg, started as soon as the fusion is identified
segments.voiceover: Remember the two key drug classes for Ph-like ALL. Ruxolitinib targets CRLF2 with JAK2 or EPOR rearrangements when MRD is high, dosed twice daily on a 2 weeks on 2 weeks off schedule. Dasatinib targets ABL class fusions like ABL1, ABL2, CSF1R, PDGFRA, or PDGFRB, and can start immediately once the fusion is found, independent of MRD status.

This is a British Journal of Haematology paper on refining risk stratification in pediatric B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia by combining IKZF1plus status with Day 15 minimal residual disease positivity. IKZF1plus refers to IKZF1 deletion occurring together with deletions in other genes such as CDKN2A, CDKN2B, PAX5, or PAR1, in the absence of ERG deletion, and it is a well-established marker of poor prognosis. The five panels show Kaplan-Meier and cumulative incidence curves comparing wild-type IKZF1, shown in red, against IKZF1 deletion, shown in blue. Panel A shows five-year event-free survival, which is clearly worse for the deletion group. Panel B shows relapse-free survival, again worse with deletion. Panel C shows overall survival, also significantly worse with deletion, all with p values less than 0.0001. Panel D looks at cumulative incidence of isolated central nervous system relapse, which shows a trend toward more events in the deletion group but does not reach statistical significance. Panel E looks at cumulative incidence of any central nervous system relapse, including combined relapses, and this difference is statistically significant. The overall message is that IKZF1 deletion, especially when combined with Day 15 MRD positivity as IKZF1plus, identifies a group of patients who need intensified therapy because their risk of relapse and death is substantially higher.

keypoints: IKZF1plus combines IKZF1 deletion with CDKN2A, CDKN2B, PAX5, or PAR1 deletion, without ERG deletion
IKZF1 deletion is associated with significantly worse 5-year event-free survival, relapse-free survival, and overall survival, all p less than 0.0001
Isolated CNS relapse trend is higher with IKZF1 deletion but not statistically significant
Any CNS relapse, including combined relapses, is significantly higher with IKZF1 deletion
segments.voiceover: For boards, know that IKZF1plus, meaning IKZF1 deletion plus other gene deletions without ERG deletion, is a strong adverse prognostic marker in B-ALL. It predicts worse event-free survival, relapse-free survival, and overall survival. Combining it with Day 15 MRD positivity sharpens risk stratification and identifies patients who need therapy intensification.

This is a British Journal of Cancer paper from a Taiwan multicenter study comparing children and adults with chronic myeloid leukemia treated with front-line imatinib. The key finding is that children have a slower molecular response than adults, even though their overall survival is comparable. The graph plots the international scale percentage of BCR-ABL1 transcript, on a log scale, against years of imatinib therapy, comparing children in black to adults in gray. Both groups start at essentially 100 percent transcript level before treatment. As therapy continues, both groups decline, but the adult curve drops faster and stays consistently lower than the children's curve at every time point from 3 months out through 13 years. The table underneath gives the median international scale percentage at each time point along with the ratio of children to adults, which is greater than 1 throughout, meaning children retain relatively more residual disease at the same time point compared to adults. This has practical implications for boards, because it means the molecular milestones you use to judge treatment response, like achieving a major molecular response by certain time points, may need to be interpreted with more patience in pediatric patients, since slower response does not necessarily mean treatment failure or the need to switch tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

keypoints: Taiwan multicenter study found children with CML on front-line imatinib have slower molecular response than adults
Children versus adults ratio of median international scale percentage remains greater than 1 at every timepoint measured
Despite slower response kinetics, overall survival in children was comparable to adults
Clinical implication is that slower molecular response in pediatric CML should not be misread as treatment failure
segments.voiceover: Key testable point is that pediatric CML patients on imatinib achieve molecular responses more slowly than adults, as shown by a persistently higher BCR-ABL1 transcript level at every timepoint. However, this slower kinetics does not translate into worse survival, so clinicians should be cautious before switching tyrosine kinase inhibitors based on response timing alone in children.

This slide continues the same Taiwan chronic myeloid leukemia study, now breaking down cumulative incidence of specific molecular response milestones over time, again comparing children in blue to adults in red. Panel A shows the cumulative incidence of reaching an international scale below 1 percent, an early response milestone. At 5 years, 75 percent of adults reach this compared to only 58 percent of children, a significant difference. Panel B shows major molecular response, roughly a 3-log reduction. At 5 years, 66 percent of adults achieve this versus 48 percent of children. Panel C shows a deeper molecular response at the 4-log level, called MR4.0. Adults reach 44 percent at 5 years and 60 percent by 8 years, while children lag at 25 percent by 5 years and 41 percent by 8 years. Panel D shows an even deeper response at the 4.5-log level, MR4.5, sometimes considered a threshold for treatment discontinuation trials. Adults reach 34 percent at 5 years and 44 percent by 10 years, while children reach only 16 percent at 5 years and 32 percent by 10 years. Every single panel shows the same consistent pattern, children take longer to reach each milestone than adults, though the gap does narrow somewhat with more years of therapy.

keypoints: Children consistently reach IS less than 1%, MMR, MR4.0, and MR4.5 milestones later than adults on front-line imatinib
At 5 years, only 58% of children versus 75% of adults reach IS less than 1%
Deep molecular response thresholds like MR4.5, relevant to treatment-free remission trials, are reached by far fewer children at 5 years, 16% versus 34% in adults
Gap between children and adults narrows somewhat with longer follow-up but persists across all response depths
segments.voiceover: For exam purposes, remember that pediatric CML patients lag behind adults at every depth of molecular response on imatinib, from early IS less than 1 percent through deep MR4.5 responses relevant to stopping therapy trials. This slower kinetics is a normal feature of pediatric CML biology, not necessarily a sign of resistance or need to escalate therapy.

This slide summarizes a Diagnostics journal article on predictors of remission in severe childhood immune thrombocytopenia, or ITP. In this cohort, about 20.9 percent of children with severe ITP went on to develop chronic ITP, meaning the disease persisted beyond 12 months. The study identified shared, significant predictors of remission that held true when assessed at the third, sixth, and twelfth month checkpoints. First, pre-adolescent age at diagnosis, specifically younger than 10 years old, favored remission. Second, an abrupt onset, defined as symptoms present for 2 weeks or less before hospital admission, favored remission, this makes intuitive sense because acute, sudden-onset ITP after a viral trigger tends to be self-limited compared to insidious onset. Third, speedy recovery, defined as a platelet count above 100 times 10 to the 9 per liter at just 1 month after diagnosis, strongly favored eventual remission. On the flip side, children who had positive viral serology tests or who had recently received a vaccination within 4 weeks of diagnosis showed a trend toward delayed remission, though this did not reach the same level of statistical significance as the three main predictors. The overall conclusion is that younger age, rapid symptom onset, and early platelet recovery are the three consistent favorable prognostic factors for remission of childhood ITP.

keypoints: About 20.9% of children with severe ITP in this cohort progressed to chronic ITP
Favorable predictors of remission at 3, 6, and 12 months: age under 10 years, abrupt onset within 2 weeks, and platelet count over 100 x10^9/L by 1 month
Positive viral serology or recent vaccination within 4 weeks trended toward delayed remission
Early platelet recovery at 1 month is one of the strongest predictors of eventual remission
segments.voiceover: For boards, memorize the three favorable predictors of remission in childhood ITP, pre-adolescent age under 10, abrupt symptom onset within 2 weeks, and platelet recovery above 100 times 10 to the 9 per liter by 1 month. These consistently predicted remission across the 3, 6, and 12 month assessment points.

This slide summarizes a British Journal of Haematology paper on the frequency and prognostic value of unconventional, meaning non-classic, genetic subtypes in pediatric and young adult B-cell precursor ALL in Taiwan. Among the unconventional subtypes, BCR-ABL1-like, also called Ph-like, is the most common, accounting for 67.3 percent of unconventional cases in children and an even higher 78.6 percent in young adults, or adolescents. There are also notable age-related differences in the underlying genetic drivers, CRLF2 rearrangement is more common in children, whereas IL7R mutations are more common in the adolescent and young adult group. Interestingly, this Taiwanese cohort had a lower overall incidence of BCR-ABL1-like disease compared to some Western cohorts, and PAX5alt subtype patients in Taiwan had a relatively better prognosis than reported elsewhere. Looking at prognosis by subtype in children, DUX4 rearranged and PAX5alt cases had favorable outcomes, while BCR-ABL1-like and MEF2D rearranged cases had poor outcomes, and both BCR-ABL1-like and MEF2D rearrangement were independent adverse prognostic factors on multivariate analysis. In adolescents and young adults, the pattern shifted, most unconventional subtypes were associated with poor prognosis in this age group, with DUX4 rearrangement being the notable exception that retained a favorable outcome.

keypoints: BCR-ABL1-like or Ph-like is the most common unconventional B-ALL subtype, 67.3% in children and 78.6% in adolescents and young adults
CRLF2 rearrangement predominates in children while IL7R mutation predominates in adolescents and young adults
In children, DUX4-R and PAX5alt predict favorable prognosis while BCR-ABL1-like and MEF2D-R are independent poor prognostic factors
In adolescents and young adults, most unconventional subtypes carry poor prognosis except DUX4-R which remains favorable
segments.voiceover: Key boards takeaway, BCR-ABL1-like or Ph-like ALL is the dominant unconventional subtype at all ages. DUX4 rearrangement is consistently a favorable marker in both children and young adults, while BCR-ABL1-like and MEF2D rearrangement are independent adverse prognostic factors, particularly emphasized in the pediatric group.

This is a diagnostic algorithm for evaluating a patient presenting with spontaneous bleeding or bruising. The workflow starts by obtaining a history for clinical clues, considering infections and acute illness which might suggest DIC, TTP, Henoch-Schonlein purpura, or hemolytic uremic syndrome, liver and nutritional causes like vitamin K or vitamin C deficiency, autoimmune or inherited conditions like von Willebrand disease, hemophilia A or B, lupus, or ITP, underlying malignancy, pregnancy, physiologic causes like senile purpura or trauma, and medications such as anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents. Next you assess a panel including CBC, PT, aPTT, Clauss fibrinogen, thrombin time, peripheral smear, and liver and kidney function. From there the algorithm branches into seven pathways based on the pattern of results. A low platelet count triggers evaluation for thrombocytopenia. Abnormally sized platelets on smear point toward platelet function testing with light transmission aggregometry, and if that's normal, you consider vascular disorders, senile purpura, connective tissue disorders like Ehlers-Danlos, amyloidosis, mild factor deficiencies, or factor XIII deficiency. Normal PT with normal aPTT and normal platelets, but with von Willebrand disease suspected, prompts checking factor VIII activity and von Willebrand antigen and activity. Normal PT with prolonged aPTT prompts a mixing study, if it corrects you check for factor VIII, IX, or XI deficiency, if it does not correct you consider an inhibitor or lupus anticoagulant. Prolonged PT with normal aPTT suggests vitamin K antagonist use, early vitamin K deficiency, or isolated factor VII deficiency. Prolonged PT and aPTT together with normal platelets suggests combined factor deficiencies, DIC, or liver disease. And prolonged PT and aPTT with low platelets points toward liver disease or DIC, remembering the pearl that in both conditions aPTT may paradoxically be normal despite elevated PT because of elevated factor VIII.

keypoints: History clues bleeding evaluation toward DIC, TTP, HSP, HUS, vitamin K or C deficiency, vWD, hemophilia, ITP, or medication effect
Initial workup includes CBC, PT, aPTT, Clauss fibrinogen, thrombin time, smear, and liver and kidney function
Isolated prolonged aPTT needs a mixing study to distinguish factor deficiency, which corrects, from an inhibitor or lupus anticoagulant, which does not correct
Prolonged PT and aPTT with thrombocytopenia suggests liver disease or DIC, and aPTT can be falsely normal due to elevated factor VIII in these conditions
segments.voiceover: For boards, master the coagulation pattern logic. Isolated prolonged aPTT that corrects on mixing study means factor VIII, IX, or XI deficiency, if it doesn't correct think inhibitor or lupus anticoagulant. Isolated prolonged PT suggests vitamin K pathway or factor VII issues. Combined PT and aPTT prolongation with thrombocytopenia should raise concern for DIC or liver disease.

This is a diagnostic algorithm for evaluation and management of thrombocytopenia in children. General causes of low platelets fall into three buckets, sequestration or pooling and dilutional issues, increased platelet destruction, and decreased platelet production. The pathway begins once platelets are below 150 times 10 to the 9 per liter.
