If platelets are below 50 times 10 to the 9 per liter, or if there is active bleeding, the child should be urgently referred to pediatric hematology right away. If not that severe, you assess CBC, reticulocyte count, mean platelet volume, and peripheral smear, making sure to rule out pseudothrombocytopenia from platelet clumping, evaluate for other cell line abnormalities suggesting bone marrow or malignant pathology, and look for schistocytes which would suggest TTP, hemolytic uremic syndrome, or DIC. From there, a series of history questions branch the workup. If other cell lines are affected, and it's limited to red blood cells, consider Evans syndrome or microangiopathic hemolytic anemia from TTP, HUS, or DIC, and refer urgently, if more than red cells are affected, consider bone marrow infiltration or failure and again refer urgently. If there's a history of eczema with small platelets, think Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. Recent rheumatologic illness points to lupus, infections like parvovirus, CMV, HIV, or hepatitis C, or lymphoproliferative disorders. Recent new medication in the past 5 to 10 days points to drug-induced thrombocytopenia, from antibiotics, antiseizure medications, aspirin, NSAIDs, or heparin. Splenomegaly points to platelet sequestration from hypersplenism or splenic vein thrombosis. A central venous catheter history points to catheter-related thrombosis. And low platelets from birth or at a young age points to Bernard-Soulier syndrome, thrombocytopenia with absent radii, MYH9-related disease, Glanzmann thrombasthenia, Fanconi anemia, or familial thrombocytopenia. If none of these apply, consider familial thrombocytopenia, vitamin B12 deficiency, vaccines, or ITP as a diagnosis of exclusion.

keypoints: Platelets below 50 x10^9/L or active bleeding warrants urgent referral to pediatric hematology
Eczema with small platelets suggests Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, a key pediatric board association
New medication within 5 to 10 days should prompt consideration of drug-induced thrombocytopenia
Thrombocytopenia present from birth or young age suggests congenital syndromes like Bernard-Soulier, TAR syndrome, MYH9-related disease, Glanzmann thrombasthenia, or Fanconi anemia
ITP remains a diagnosis of exclusion after other causes are ruled out
segments.voiceover: For boards, key pattern recognition points, eczema plus small platelets equals Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, congenital onset thrombocytopenia should trigger workup for Bernard-Soulier, TAR syndrome, MYH9 disorders, Glanzmann thrombasthenia, or Fanconi anemia, and always rule out drug causes and other etiologies before labeling a child's thrombocytopenia as ITP, since ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion.

This flowchart gives you a practical approach when you suspect an inherited platelet disorder. You always start with a CBC and peripheral blood smear. If the platelet count is normal, you check von Willebrand studies first, and if those are normal too, you move on to platelet aggregation testing, which can show a nonspecific pattern pointing toward acquired or mild disorders, or a significant abnormal pattern that splits into granule release defects like storage pool disease, or surface protein defects like Glanzmann thrombasthenia or Bernard Soulier syndrome. If instead the patient has thrombocytopenia, the mean platelet volume becomes your key branch point. Large platelets with an M P V under twelve suggest MYH9 related disorder, Paris Trousseau Jacobsen syndrome, or twenty two q deletion syndrome, and these go straight to genetic analysis. Normal sized platelets point toward bone marrow failure syndromes such as congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia, thrombocytopenia absent radius, or familial platelet disorder with AML predisposition, which need a bone marrow study before genetics. Small platelets under six femtoliters should make you think of Wiskott Aldrich syndrome or X linked thrombocytopenia, worked up with immune function studies.

keypoints: Start every workup with CBC and peripheral smear
Normal platelet count pathway checks von Willebrand studies then aggregation
Thrombocytopenia pathway branches by mean platelet volume
Large platelets suggest MYH9 related disorder or Paris Trousseau syndrome
Small platelets suggest Wiskott Aldrich syndrome or X linked thrombocytopenia
segments.voiceover: Remember this algorithm by starting with CBC and smear, then splitting into normal platelet count versus thrombocytopenia. For thrombocytopenia, mean platelet volume is the key branch point, large platelets suggest MYH9 related disease, normal size suggests marrow failure syndromes, and small platelets point toward Wiskott Aldrich or X linked thrombocytopenia.

This table organizes familial thrombocytopenias by platelet size, and then splits each size category into syndromic forms, meaning there are other clinical features besides low platelets, versus non syndromic forms, where thrombocytopenia is essentially isolated. For giant platelets, the syndromic entity is MYH9 related disease, which includes May Hegglin anomaly, Sebastian, Fechtner, and Epstein syndromes, while the non syndromic counterpart is biallelic Bernard Soulier syndrome or TUBB1 related thrombocytopenia. For large platelets, syndromic causes include Paris Trousseau thrombocytopenia syndrome and GATA1 related disease, while non syndromic causes include monoallelic Bernard Soulier syndrome, gray platelet syndrome, and Glanzmann thrombasthenia. When platelet size is normal, syndromic causes include thrombocytopenia with absent radii and amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia with radio ulnar synostosis, while non syndromic causes include congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia and familial platelet disorder with predisposition to AML, involving genes like ANKRD26, CYCS, and ETV6. Finally, for small platelets, the classic syndromic entity is Wiskott Aldrich syndrome and X linked thrombocytopenia, which for boards is a very testable, high yield association.

keypoints: Organize familial thrombocytopenias by platelet size then syndromic versus non syndromic
Giant platelets: MYH9 related disease is the classic syndromic cause
Large platelets: Paris Trousseau and GATA1 related disease are syndromic
Normal size: thrombocytopenia absent radii and CAMT are key entities
Small platelets: Wiskott Aldrich syndrome is the classic syndromic cause
segments.voiceover: For boards, memorize this table using platelet size as your anchor. Giant platelets point to MYH9 related disease, large platelets point to Paris Trousseau or GATA1 related disease, normal size points to TAR and congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia, and small platelets point to Wiskott Aldrich syndrome.

This table classifies inherited platelet disorders by the specific platelet component that is abnormal, which is a really useful framework for boards because it links mechanism directly to disease name. Abnormalities of the platelet receptors for adhesive proteins involve the GPIb IX V complex, causing Bernard Soulier syndrome and platelet type von Willebrand disease, or GPIIb IIIa, also written alpha IIb beta three, causing Glanzmann thrombasthenia, these two are highlighted because they are the most testable. Abnormalities of receptors for soluble agonists involve P2Y12 or thromboxane A2 receptors, causing the respective receptor deficiencies. Abnormalities of platelet granules are split into delta granule problems, which include nonsyndromic delta storage pool deficiency, Hermansky Pudlak syndrome, and Chediak Higashi syndrome, and alpha granule problems, which include gray platelet syndrome and several rarer entities. Further down, defects of signal transduction, abnormalities of membrane phospholipids like Scott syndrome, and miscellaneous causes round out the classification. The two red underlined rows, Bernard Soulier syndrome, Glanzmann thrombasthenia, and Chediak Higashi syndrome, are emphasized because they are the highest yield for exam purposes.

keypoints: Classification is organized by which platelet component is abnormal
GPIb IX V complex defect causes Bernard Soulier syndrome
GPIIb IIIa defect causes Glanzmann thrombasthenia
Delta granule defects include Hermansky Pudlak and Chediak Higashi syndromes
Alpha granule defect is exemplified by gray platelet syndrome
segments.voiceover: Anchor this table to two receptor defects. GPIb IX V complex deficiency gives you Bernard Soulier syndrome, and GPIIb IIIa deficiency gives you Glanzmann thrombasthenia. Then remember delta granule defects like Chediak Higashi and Hermansky Pudlak, and alpha granule defect meaning gray platelet syndrome.

This table compares the clinical and laboratory features of several inherited platelet function disorders, and it is exactly the kind of table boards love to test with vignette style questions. Glanzmann thrombasthenia has a normal platelet count and normal size, but shows absent aggregation with all agonists except ristocetin, which is the classic distinguishing lab clue, it is autosomal recessive and involves ITGA2B or ITGB3. GPVI collagen receptor defect and P2Y12 ADP receptor defect are both autosomal recessive with normal counts and size but specific aggregation abnormalities to their respective agonists. Thromboxane A2 receptor defect is autosomal dominant. Then we get to the two storage pool diseases with associated syndromes, Chediak Higashi syndrome, which features albinism, eczema, recurrent infections, and lymphohistiocytosis, caused by LYST mutations, and Hermansky Pudlak syndrome, which features albinism plus pulmonary fibrosis and lysosomal storage disease, caused by several HPS genes. Scott syndrome has entirely normal aggregation testing because the defect is in membrane phospholipid scrambling, not aggregation. Finally, Bernard Soulier syndrome stands out because it is the only one here with a decreased platelet count and large platelets, showing absent aggregation specifically with ristocetin but normal response to other agonists, essentially the mirror image of Glanzmann.

keypoints: Glanzmann thrombasthenia: absent aggregation to all agonists except ristocetin
Bernard Soulier syndrome: absent aggregation only with ristocetin, large platelets, low count
Chediak Higashi syndrome pairs platelet dysfunction with albinism and recurrent infections
Hermansky Pudlak syndrome pairs platelet dysfunction with albinism and pulmonary fibrosis
Scott syndrome has normal aggregation because the defect is phospholipid scrambling
segments.voiceover: The single most testable contrast here is Glanzmann versus Bernard Soulier. Glanzmann loses aggregation to everything except ristocetin, while Bernard Soulier loses aggregation only to ristocetin and has large platelets with a low count. Also remember Chediak Higashi and Hermansky Pudlak as the two syndromic delta granule disorders with albinism.

This is a continuation of the same table, now covering entities with decreased platelet counts and various clinical syndromes. Gray platelet syndrome shows large pale platelets with absent alpha granules, heterogeneous response to agonists, and is associated with myelofibrosis and pulmonary fibrosis, caused by NBEAL2, inherited as autosomal recessive or dominant. Wiskott Aldrich syndrome, highlighted here, has decreased count with small platelets and delta granule deficiency, impaired aggregation, and the classic clinical triad of eczema, infections, and immunodeficiency plus autoimmune disease and malignancy risk, it is X linked and caused by the WAS gene, this is extremely high yield. Then we move into the bone marrow failure group, all with normal platelet size and normal function but decreased count. Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia involves MPL and leads to bone marrow failure. Thrombocytopenia absent radii features decreased megakaryocytes with limb abnormalities. Amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia with radio ulnar synostosis involves HOXA11 with skeletal abnormalities and hearing loss. Familial platelet disorder with predisposition to AML involves RUNX1. Paris Trousseau Jacobsen syndrome features large platelets with large granules, pancytopenia, and facial and cardiac anomalies, involving ETS1 and FLT1. And GATA1 mutation causes X linked thrombocytopenia with thalassemia and anemia.

keypoints: Gray platelet syndrome: large pale platelets missing alpha granules, NBEAL2 gene
Wiskott Aldrich syndrome: small platelets, eczema, infections, immunodeficiency, X linked
CAMT and TAR both present with decreased count and normal platelet size
FPD AML involves RUNX1 and predisposes to myelodysplasia and leukemia
Paris Trousseau syndrome features large platelets with large granules plus facial and cardiac anomalies
segments.voiceover: Focus on Wiskott Aldrich syndrome as the highest yield entity on this slide, small platelets, X linked, and the eczema infection immunodeficiency triad. Then remember gray platelet syndrome for absent alpha granules, and RUNX1 mutation for familial platelet disorder with AML predisposition, a classic germline leukemia predisposition syndrome.

Glanzmann thrombasthenia, or platelet weakness disease, results from mutations in the ITGA2B or ITGB3 genes located on chromosome seventeen, which together encode the GPIIb IIIa receptor complex. The gel image on the right nicely demonstrates this, showing that the Glanzmann sample is missing the GPII and GPIII bands compared to the control lane. Severity is graded by residual receptor expression, mild disease has greater than twenty percent, moderate disease is five to twenty percent, and severe disease is less than five percent. For management, mild mucocutaneous bleeding can often be controlled with antifibrinolytics, either intravenous Amicar or oral Cyklokapron. Women with heavy menstrual bleeding may benefit from oral contraceptive pills to reduce flow. In June twenty fourteen, the FDA approved recombinant factor seven a, brand name NovoSeven RT, specifically for Glanzmann patients who are refractory to platelets or who have platelet antibodies. For severe, life threatening bleeding episodes, platelet transfusion remains the definitive treatment, though repeated transfusions carry a risk of alloimmunization.

keypoints: Caused by ITGA2B or ITGB3 mutations affecting the GPIIb IIIa complex on chromosome 17
Severity graded by residual GP expression: mild over 20%, moderate 5 to 20%, severe under 5%
First line for mild bleeding is antifibrinolytics, Amicar or Cyklokapron
Recombinant factor seven a, NovoSeven RT, FDA approved in 2014 for refractory cases
Platelet transfusion is used for severe bleeding despite alloimmunization risk
segments.voiceover: Key points for boards, Glanzmann thrombasthenia comes from GPIIb IIIa deficiency due to ITGA2B or ITGB3 mutations. Treat mild bleeding with antifibrinolytics, consider recombinant factor seven a for refractory bleeding, and reserve platelet transfusion for severe hemorrhage.

Bernard Soulier syndrome results from a lack of the glycoprotein GPIb IX complex, more precisely a deficiency of the GPIb IX V complex, which you can see illustrated in the diagram sitting on the platelet membrane. This complex is the platelet's primary receptor for von Willebrand factor, and it also interacts with collagen, factor eleven, factor twelve, thrombin, thrombospondin, and kininogen, so when it is missing, platelets cannot properly adhere to the vessel wall under high shear conditions. Clinically this translates into two hallmark laboratory findings, a decreased platelet count, so this is a true thrombocytopenia unlike Glanzmann thrombasthenia, and large platelets greater than four micrometers in diameter on the peripheral smear. On aggregation studies, remember that Bernard Soulier syndrome shows absent aggregation specifically in response to ristocetin, while aggregation to other agonists like ADP and collagen remains normal, this is the opposite pattern from Glanzmann thrombasthenia and is a classic board discriminator.

keypoints: Bernard Soulier syndrome is caused by GPIb IX V complex deficiency
GPIb IX V is the platelet receptor for von Willebrand factor
Presents with decreased platelet count, unlike Glanzmann thrombasthenia
Large platelets greater than 4 micrometers on peripheral smear
Absent ristocetin induced aggregation but normal response to other agonists
segments.voiceover: Remember Bernard Soulier syndrome as GPIb IX V deficiency causing loss of von Willebrand factor binding. It presents with a low platelet count and giant platelets, and on aggregation studies it fails only with ristocetin, the mirror image of Glanzmann thrombasthenia.

Wiskott Aldrich syndrome is X linked recessive, so it classically presents in young boys, and the mnemonic WAITER is a great way to remember its features for boards. W is for Wiskott, A is for Aldrich, I stands for immunodeficiency, T stands for thrombocytopenia, E stands for eczema, and R stands for recurrent pyogenic infection. The images on this slide illustrate each of these, the chest x ray shows pneumonia and other recurrent infections from the immunodeficiency, the histology panel shows B cell lymphoma and other malignancies that these patients are predisposed to over time, the photo of the shoulder shows petechiae from thrombocytopenia, and the facial photo shows the characteristic eczema. Remember that the platelets in Wiskott Aldrich syndrome are small, which helps distinguish it from Bernard Soulier syndrome where platelets are large, even though both cause thrombocytopenia. The definitive treatment is hematopoietic stem cell transplant, which can correct the immunodeficiency and thrombocytopenia and reduce the malignancy risk if performed early.

keypoints: X linked recessive disorder presenting in young boys
Mnemonic WAITER: Wiskott, Aldrich, Immunodeficiency, Thrombocytopenia, Eczema, Recurrent infection
Small platelets distinguish it from Bernard Soulier syndrome's large platelets
Increased risk of B cell lymphoma and other malignancies over time
Definitive treatment is hematopoietic stem cell transplant
segments.voiceover: Use the WAITER mnemonic to lock in Wiskott Aldrich syndrome, Wiskott, Aldrich, immunodeficiency, thrombocytopenia, eczema, and recurrent pyogenic infection. It is X linked with small platelets, and definitive treatment is hematopoietic stem cell transplant.

This table compares the four classic inherited platelet disorders that show up again and again on boards. Bernard Soulier syndrome gives you a low platelet count, often thirty to two hundred times ten to the third per microliter, with large platelets, and it's caused by mutations in G P one B A, G P one B B, or G P nine, inherited autosomal recessive. The defect is in the G P one b nine five complex, so platelets can't bind von Willebrand factor and adhesion fails. Contrast that with Glanzmann thrombasthenia, where the platelet count and size are both normal, but mutations in I T G A two B or I T G B three knock out the G P two b three a receptor, alpha two b beta three, so platelets can't aggregate even though they adhere fine. Chediak Higashi syndrome, caused by L Y S T mutations, gives normal or mildly low platelets with a dense granule deficiency that impairs storage and secretion, and remember this one comes with oculocutaneous albinism and giant cytoplasmic granules in leukocytes. Finally Wiskott Aldrich syndrome is X linked recessive, caused by W A S mutations, and it's the one with small platelets and thrombocytopenia from a cytoskeletal defect affecting platelet production and function. The classic triad to remember is thrombocytopenia, eczema, and recurrent infections.

keypoints: Bernard Soulier: low count, large platelets, GP1b-IX-V defect, autosomal recessive
Glanzmann thrombasthenia: normal count and size, GPIIb/IIIa defect, impaired aggregation
Chediak-Higashi: LYST mutation, dense granule deficiency, albinism association
Wiskott-Aldrich: X-linked, small platelets, cytoskeletal defect, triad with eczema and infection
segments.voiceover: Four inherited platelet disorders. Bernard Soulier is large platelets with a G P one b defect and impaired adhesion. Glanzmann thrombasthenia has normal size platelets but a G P two b three a defect causing impaired aggregation. Chediak Higashi involves L Y S T mutations with dense granule deficiency, linked to albinism. And Wiskott Aldrich is X linked with small platelets, a cytoskeletal defect, and the classic triad of thrombocytopenia, eczema, and recurrent infections.

Histiocytosis syndromes result from excess proliferation and accumulation of dendritic cells, monocytes, and macrophages, sometimes along with eosinophils and lymphocytes, depending on the specific subtype. The World Health Organization classification splits these into three types. Type one covers dendritic cell disorders, and this is where Langerhans cell histiocytosis, or L C H, lives, including the older names you might still see on boards, like eosinophilic granuloma for localized bone disease, Hand Schuller Christian syndrome for multisystem disease with bone involvement, diabetes insipidus, and exophthalmos, and Abt Letterer Siwe syndrome for the disseminated form with risk organ dysfunction. Also in type one are juvenile xanthogranulomatosis and Erdheim Chester disease. Type two covers macrophage related disorders, and this is the hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis family, including familial and infection associated and malignancy associated hemophagocytic syndromes, plus Rosai Dorfman disease. Type three is the malignant histiocytic disorders, like dendritic cell related or macrophage related histiocytic sarcoma, and monocytic leukemia or sarcoma. For boards, the key organizing principle is: type one is dendritic cell, type two is macrophage and hemophagocytic, type three is frankly malignant.

keypoints: Type I: dendritic cell disorders, includes LCH (formerly eosinophilic granuloma, Hand-Schuller-Christian, Letterer-Siwe)
Type II: macrophage-related disorders, includes HLH and Rosai-Dorfman disease
Type III: malignant histiocytic disorders, includes histiocytic sarcoma and monocytic leukemia
Classification driven by which immune effector cell proliferates: dendritic cell, macrophage, or malignant clone
segments.voiceover: Remember the three WHO types of histiocytosis. Type one is dendritic cell disorders, home of Langerhans cell histiocytosis and its old eponyms. Type two is macrophage related disorders, which includes hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and Rosai Dorfman disease. Type three is the malignant histiocytic disorders, like histiocytic sarcoma.

This is the diagnostic framework for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, based on the revised Histiocyte Society HLH 2004 study and reflected in the T P O G HLH 2025 protocol. You can establish the diagnosis if any one of three pathways is fulfilled. Pathway A is a molecular diagnosis consistent with familial HLH in a patient with suggestive signs and symptoms, meaning a pathogenic biallelic mutation in one of the known genes: P R F one, U N C thirteen D, S T X eleven, S T X B P two, L Y S T, R A B twenty seven A, S H two D one A, X I A P, or N L R C four. Pathway B is functional cellular findings consistent with familial HLH. And pathway C, the one tested most often, requires five out of seven clinical and laboratory criteria. Those seven are: fever of thirty eight point five Celsius or higher; splenomegaly at least two centimeters below the costal margin; cytopenia affecting at least two of three lineages, meaning hemoglobin under nine, platelets under one hundred thousand, or neutrophils under one thousand; hypertriglyceridemia at or above three millimoles per liter, or hypofibrinogenemia at or below one hundred fifty milligrams per deciliter; hemophagocytosis seen on bone marrow, spleen, or lymph node biopsy without evidence of malignancy; hyperferritinemia at or above five hundred micrograms per liter; and soluble C D twenty five, the soluble interleukin two receptor, at or above twenty four hundred units per milliliter. Memorizing this five of seven list cold is essential for boards.

keypoints: HLH diagnosis: molecular diagnosis (A), functional findings (B), or 5 of 7 clinical criteria (C)
5 of 7 criteria: fever, splenomegaly, bicytopenia, hypertriglyceridemia or hypofibrinogenemia, hemophagocytosis, hyperferritinemia, elevated soluble CD25
Genetic HLH genes include PRF1, UNC13D, STX11, STXBP2, RAB27A, LYST, SH2D1A, XIAP, NLRC4
This is the HLH-2004 criteria set, still the backbone of current TPOG protocols
segments.voiceover: HLH can be diagnosed by a molecular diagnosis, by functional cellular findings, or by meeting five of seven clinical and lab criteria. Those seven are fever, splenomegaly, cytopenia in two or more lineages, hypertriglyceridemia or low fibrinogen, hemophagocytosis on biopsy, high ferritin, and elevated soluble C D twenty five. Know this five of seven list cold for boards.

This flowchart walks through the practical workup once HLH is suspected. You branch into two parallel tracks. On one side you ask about previous HLH, a positive family history, or a known genetic mutation. On the other side you evaluate for mimics: malignancies, infections, rheumatologic disease, and other primary immune deficiencies, since secondary HLH triggers need to be ruled in or out. Both tracks converge on the question of whether ferritin and or soluble C D twenty five are elevated. If no, HLH is unlikely, except in cases of isolated central nervous system disease, which can present without the typical systemic lab abnormalities. If yes, you move into the full diagnostic evaluation panel. General HLH studies include a C B C, A L T and bilirubin, fibrinogen and coagulation tests, triglycerides, ferritin and soluble C D twenty five, and where available C X C L nine, interleukin eighteen, and T cell H L A D R, plus a bone marrow or other tissue aspirate and biopsy to look for hemophagocytosis. CNS evaluation includes a brain M R I and lumbar puncture, since CNS involvement changes management. Adjunctive studies include C T of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, P E T C T to evaluate for lymphoma, viral P C Rs for E B V, C M V, adenovirus, and H S V, and consideration of tick or mosquito borne disease testing. Rapid screening tests for primary HLH include perforin, S A P, X I A P, and C D one oh seven a expression, followed by genetic testing to confirm a familial form.

keypoints: Two parallel entry points: prior HLH or genetic mutation, versus workup for malignancy, infection, rheumatologic disease
Elevated ferritin and/or soluble CD25 triggers full diagnostic evaluation; if not elevated, HLH is unlikely except isolated CNS disease
General studies: CBC, LFTs, fibrinogen, triglycerides, ferritin, sCD25, CXCL9, IL-18, marrow biopsy for hemophagocytosis
Rapid functional screening: perforin, SAP, XIAP, CD107a expression, followed by confirmatory genetic testing
segments.voiceover: When HLH is suspected, check ferritin and soluble C D twenty five first. If they're not elevated, HLH is unlikely unless there's isolated CNS disease. If elevated, proceed to general HLH labs, CNS imaging with brain M R I and lumbar puncture, infectious workup, and rapid functional screening tests like perforin, S A P, X I A P, and C D one oh seven a, followed by genetic testing to confirm.

This slide flags two important treatment topics for HLH: the role and use of ruxolitinib, and the timing of hematopoietic stem cell transplant. Ruxolitinib is a Janus kinase one and two inhibitor that's increasingly used in relapsed or refractory HLH, because it blunts the cytokine storm driven by interferon gamma and other JAK STAT dependent cytokines that fuel the hyperinflammatory state. For transplant timing, the key concept is that genetic HLH is the group that ultimately needs a hematopoietic stem cell transplant for cure, since the underlying defect is in the cytotoxic machinery of T cells and N K cells. Genetic HLH includes patients with pathogenic variants in P R F one, U N C thirteen D, S T X eleven, S T X B P two, R A B twenty seven A, L Y S T, S H two D one A, and N L R C four, and also some patients with X I A P deficiency. Once a patient is identified as having genetic or familial HLH, or has relapsing disease, transplant referral should happen promptly after disease control is achieved with induction therapy, because delaying transplant risks disease reactivation and organ damage.

keypoints: Ruxolitinib: JAK1/2 inhibitor used in relapsed or refractory HLH to dampen cytokine storm
HSCT is curative therapy for genetic (familial) HLH
Genetic HLH genes: PRF1, UNC13D, STX11, STXBP2, RAB27A, LYST, SH2D1A, NLRC4, and some XIAP deficiency
Early transplant referral after induction control reduces risk of relapse and organ damage
segments.voiceover: Two key management points. Ruxolitinib, a JAK one two inhibitor, is used for relapsed or refractory HLH to control the cytokine storm. And hematopoietic stem cell transplant is the definitive cure for genetic HLH, which includes mutations in genes like P R F one, U N C thirteen D, and several others, plus some X I A P deficient patients, and transplant should be pursued promptly once disease is controlled.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis, or L C H, is defined as a clonal neoplasm arising from an immature dendritic cell, or in some cases from an earlier hematopoietic precursor cell. Pathologically, the diagnostic markers on immunohistochemistry are C D one a and C D two oh seven, also called langerin, which is the Langerhans cell antigen. On electron microscopy, the classic finding is Birbeck granules, which have a distinctive tennis racket shape. In terms of pathogenesis, this is a RAS RAF MEK ERK pathway disease, driven by B R A F V six hundred E mutations in fifty to sixty percent of cases, which activates that MAP kinase signaling cascade. For risk stratification, the critical distinction is risk organs versus not: the hematopoietic system, liver, spleen, and lung count as risk organs, and involvement here changes prognosis and treatment intensity. There's also a special site category covering vertebral lesions and CNS risk lesions, which need closer monitoring even without classic risk organ involvement, plus a category for organ dysfunction. Treatment depends entirely on which sites are involved, ranging from observation for a single lesion, to steroids, to systemic chemotherapy for multisystem or risk organ disease. The five year overall survival is good for low risk patients, meaning those without risk organ involvement, but worse for those with risk organ dysfunction at diagnosis.

keypoints: LCH: clonal dendritic cell neoplasm; IHC positive for CD1a and CD207 (langerin); EM shows Birbeck granules
Pathogenesis: BRAF V600E mutation in 50-60%, activating RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK pathway
Risk organs are hematopoietic system, liver, spleen, and lung; special sites include vertebral and CNS-risk lesions
Treatment and prognosis depend on site involvement; low-risk (no risk-organ) patients have good 5-year survival
segments.voiceover: L C H is a clonal dendritic cell neoplasm, positive for C D one a and C D two oh seven on immunohistochemistry, with Birbeck granules on electron microscopy. Roughly half to sixty percent have a B R A F V six hundred E mutation activating the RAS RAF MEK ERK pathway. Risk organs are hematopoietic system, liver, spleen, and lung, and their involvement drives both treatment intensity and prognosis.

This flowchart shows the risk classification and treatment algorithm from the T P O G L C H twenty twenty three protocol. At the top, disease splits into multisystem versus single system, excluding critical organs. Multisystem disease further splits by risk organ status: multiple system multiple site with risk organ positive, meaning liver, spleen, or bone marrow involvement, versus risk organ negative, which can still include multifocal bone lesions. Single system disease splits into single system multiple site, single specific site involving weight bearing bone or CNS risk bone, and single site without fever, which goes straight to local therapy alone. Everyone else starts induction therapy one. For the risk organ positive group, there's an early evaluation at day fourteen to twenty one, while the other multisystem and single system multiple site groups are evaluated at the end of induction one, around day thirty five to forty two. Based on response, categorized as better, worse, others, or N A D meaning no active disease, patients either move to maintenance, continue with a second line approach, or proceed to induction therapy two. Importantly, all CNS risk bone lesions require induction therapy two regardless of the day thirty five response, because of the risk of CNS complications like diabetes insipidus. After induction two, response is reevaluated again, and patients who are others or worse may escalate to second or even third line therapy, while those who are better or greater proceed to maintenance. Maintenance duration is twelve months for multifocal bone disease only, and twenty four months for everyone else.

keypoints: Multisystem disease with risk organ (liver/spleen/marrow) positive gets early evaluation at D14-21
Others get evaluated at end of induction 1 (D35-42): response graded as NAD, better/worse, or others
CNS risk bone lesions always require induction therapy 2 regardless of D35 response
Maintenance: 12 months for multifocal bone only, 24 months for all other risk groups
segments.voiceover: The T P O G L C H twenty twenty three algorithm stratifies by multisystem versus single system disease and by risk organ status. Risk organ positive patients get an early day fourteen to twenty one evaluation, everyone else is evaluated at the end of induction one around day thirty five. All CNS risk bone lesions get induction therapy two no matter the response. And maintenance runs twelve months for multifocal bone only disease, but twenty four months for all other groups.

This is a nice visual summary of Langerhans cell histiocytosis and where it shows up in the body. The disease is an excess of immature Langerhans cells, which are antigen presenting immune cells normally found in the skin, forming granulomas across multiple organs. About fifty percent of cases carry a somatic B R A F mutation, prevalence is roughly one to two per one hundred thousand, with a two to one male to female ratio, and it's most commonly diagnosed in children age one to three. Clinically, children tend to present with acute disseminated multisystem disease, while adults and older children more often have indolent single organ disease. Going organ by organ: bone granulomas are the most common finding at seventy seven percent, typically in the skull and long bones, causing pain, swelling, and fractures, and you'll often see a classic punched out lytic skull lesion on X ray. Skin and mucosal granulomas occur in thirty nine percent, presenting as blisters, papules, or a maculopapular rash, classically a scaly eczematous diaper rash that's refractory to standard treatment. Lymph node and bone marrow granulomas occur in nineteen percent, causing lymphadenopathy and pancytopenia. CNS and pituitary granulomas occur in only six percent but are high yield for boards, causing headache, dizziness, proptosis, seizures, and critically diabetes insipidus from loss of A D H, plus growth hormone loss, pubertal delay from G n R H deficiency, and hypothyroidism from T S H loss. Lung granulomas occur in ten percent, more common in adult smokers, causing respiratory distress, pneumothorax, chronic cough, and weight loss. Liver granulomas occur in sixteen percent with jaundice, elevated transaminases, ascites, hypoalbuminemia, and factor deficiencies, and splenic granulomas occur in thirteen percent causing splenomegaly. Diagnosis is by biopsy of the granuloma with immunohistochemical staining and electron microscopy, and treatment includes prednisone, vinblastine, curettage of bone lesions, and topical therapy for skin disease.

keypoints: Bone involvement is most common (77%): skull and long bones, classic punched-out lytic lesions
Diabetes insipidus from CNS/pituitary involvement (6%) is a high-yield board finding, along with growth hormone and TSH loss
Classic infant presentation: scaly, eczematous diaper rash refractory to standard treatment
Diagnosis: biopsy with IHC and electron microscopy; treatment: prednisone, vinblastine, curettage, topical therapy
segments.voiceover: L C H most commonly affects bone, at seventy seven percent, giving punched out lytic skull lesions. CNS and pituitary involvement is rarer, around six percent, but is board favorite because of diabetes insipidus and other pituitary hormone losses. A refractory eczematous diaper rash is a classic infant clue. Diagnosis rests on biopsy with immunohistochemistry and electron microscopy, and treatment is prednisone and vinblastine, plus local measures for bone or skin lesions.

This slide gives you the overview of pediatric brain tumors that you need for boards. On the left, the classic Nelson's diagram breaks hemispheric tumors down into gliomas, which make up thirty seven percent, split into low grade astrocytomas at twenty three percent and high grade astrocytomas at eleven percent. In the midline, chiasmal gliomas run about four percent, craniopharyngiomas eight percent, and pineal region tumors two percent. In the posterior fossa, you have four roughly equal big hitters, brainstem gliomas, medulloblastomas, and cerebellar astrocytomas each around fifteen percent, with ependymomas at four percent. On the right is a Taiwanese cohort pie chart showing low grade gliomas as the single largest group at thirty two percent, followed by germ cell tumors fourteen percent, medulloblastoma thirteen percent, high grade glioma nine percent, and craniopharyngioma eight percent. The high yield takeaway for boards is that posterior fossa tumors dominate childhood, while low grade gliomas are actually the most common single histology overall, and medulloblastoma and pineal region tumors are the two entries highlighted here because they come up repeatedly in exam questions.

keypoints: Gliomas are the most common hemispheric brain tumor category, thirty seven percent
Posterior fossa tumors, brainstem glioma, medulloblastoma, cerebellar astrocytoma, each about fifteen percent
Low grade glioma is the single most common histology overall, around thirty two percent
Medulloblastoma and pineal region tumors are exam favorites
segments.voiceover: Remember three things for boards. Gliomas dominate the hemispheres at thirty seven percent. The posterior fossa is split roughly evenly between brainstem glioma, medulloblastoma, and cerebellar astrocytoma. And across all locations, low grade glioma is the single most common pediatric brain tumor type.

This slide makes two points about pediatric brain tumor epidemiology. The top bar chart compares incidence rates per hundred thousand across eight countries and registries, the United States, Australia, the UK, Japan, Singapore, China, Korea, and Taiwan. You can see meaningful variation in total incidence and in the relative proportion of astrocytoma, embryonal tumors like medulloblastoma and PNET, other gliomas, germ cell tumors, and ependymoma between these populations, which is a reminder that epidemiologic data isn't fully generalizable across regions. The bottom chart is more testable, it shows brain tumor type by age band, under one, one to four, five to nine, ten to fourteen, and fifteen to nineteen. Notice that embryonal tumors, the purple segment, are proportionally much larger in the youngest age groups, under one and one to four, and then shrink with age, while astrocytoma, the orange segment, becomes proportionally dominant by the teenage years. CNS germ cell tumors also show an age pattern, becoming more prominent in the five to nine and ten to fourteen bands. The board relevant lesson is that age at presentation should shift your differential, embryonal tumors like medulloblastoma cluster in infants and young children, astrocytomas and gliomas become relatively more common as children get older.

keypoints: Brain tumor incidence and subtype distribution vary by country and registry
Embryonal tumors, like medulloblastoma, are proportionally most common in infants and toddlers
Astrocytoma becomes the dominant subtype by the teenage years
Use age at presentation to help narrow your brain tumor differential
segments.voiceover: Two things to lock in. First, incidence rates and tumor subtype proportions genuinely differ across countries and registries. Second, and more testable, age shapes the differential, embryonal tumors like medulloblastoma peak in infants and young children, while astrocytoma becomes proportionally dominant as kids move into adolescence.

This is a classic boards table pairing cancer predisposition syndromes with their associated CNS tumor types, and it's worth memorizing the highlighted rows. Hereditary retinoblastoma, caused by Rb mutations, predisposes to pineoblastoma, glioma, and meningioma, plus non CNS tumors like osteosarcoma and melanoma. Li Fraumeni syndrome, from TP53 mutations, is associated with multiple brain tumor types, most classically supratentorial PNET, medulloblastoma, and astrocytoma, along with sarcomas, adrenocortical tumors, leukemia, and early breast cancer. Neurofibromatosis type one, NF1 gene, causes optic nerve glioma and astrocytoma, while neurofibromatosis type two, the NF2 gene, causes bilateral acoustic schwannomas, meningiomas, and spinal ependymomas, that bilateral acoustic schwannoma finding is the classic NF2 board buzzword. Beyond the highlighted rows, remember Cowden syndrome with PTEN causing dysplastic cerebellar gangliocytoma, also called Lhermitte Duclos disease, Gorlin syndrome with PTCH causing medulloblastoma and basal cell carcinomas, tuberous sclerosis with TSC1 or TSC2 causing subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, Turcot syndrome with APC or the mismatch repair genes causing medulloblastoma or astrocytoma with colorectal tumors, and von Hippel Lindau with the VHL gene causing hemangioblastoma.

keypoints: Li Fraumeni, TP53, causes multiple brain tumors including medulloblastoma and astrocytoma
NF2 causes bilateral acoustic schwannoma, a classic board buzzword
Tuberous sclerosis causes subependymal giant cell astrocytoma
Von Hippel Lindau causes hemangioblastoma
segments.voiceover: The highest yield pairings here are Li Fraumeni and TP53 with multiple brain tumor types including medulloblastoma, neurofibromatosis type two with bilateral acoustic schwannoma, tuberous sclerosis with subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, and von Hippel Lindau with hemangioblastoma. Match the gene to the tumor and you'll cover most exam questions on this topic.

This slide covers NF1 diagnostic criteria and a Taiwan specific reimbursement update. For the diagnosis of NF1, a patient needs two or more of eight criteria, and this list is worth knowing cold for boards. First, a family history of NF1 in a first degree relative. Second, six or more café au lait macules, greater than zero point five centimeters before puberty or greater than one point five centimeters after puberty. Third, two or more neurofibromas or one plexiform neurofibroma. Fourth, freckling in the axillary or inguinal regions. Fifth, iris Lisch nodules, two or more, which are hamartomas that don't affect vision. Sixth, a distinctive bony lesion such as sphenoid dysplasia or long bone cortical thinning, which can present as bowing of the legs. Seventh, bilateral optic nerve gliomas, which rarely affect vision. And these criteria, taken together, two or more of the eight, establish the diagnosis, though formal confirmation should always come from a specialist. The bottom of the slide is a local practice note, in Taiwan, selumetinib, brand name Koselugo, became covered by National Health Insurance in February of twenty twenty five for patients aged three to eighteen with a confirmed diagnosis of neurofibromatosis type one who have inoperable, symptomatic plexiform neurofibromas, this reflects the same MEK inhibitor indication used internationally for progressive plexiform neurofibromas.

keypoints: NF1 diagnosis requires two or more of eight clinical criteria
Six or more café au lait macules is the most recognizable criterion
Lisch nodules are iris hamartomas that do not impair vision
Selumetinib, Koselugo, treats inoperable symptomatic plexiform neurofibromas in NF1
segments.voiceover: For NF1, know that diagnosis needs two of eight criteria, with café au lait macules, neurofibromas, axillary or inguinal freckling, Lisch nodules, optic glioma, and characteristic bone lesions being the classic exam list. Therapeutically, selumetinib is the MEK inhibitor now used for inoperable, symptomatic plexiform neurofibromas in NF1 patients.

Medulloblastoma is the prototypical embryonal tumor of childhood, and this table organizes exactly what you need for boards. Primary site is the cerebellum. On special exam, brain MRI classically shows a solid, homogeneously enhancing mass in the posterior fossa, and because thirty percent of patients have leptomeningeal spread at diagnosis, staging always requires whole spine MRI and lumbar puncture for CSF cytology. Risk stratification uses three inputs, age, the preoperative Chang staging system which looks at tumor size, local extension, and metastases, and postoperative factors including extent of residual tumor, histology, and molecular subtype. The table two three point eight spells out the classic average risk versus high risk criteria, average risk means negative CSF cytology, a normal spine MRI, less than one point five square centimeters of residual tumor, undifferentiated histology, and age greater than three years, while high risk means positive CSF cytology, positive spine MRI, greater than one point five square centimeters residual, large cell anaplastic histology, and age less than three years. Molecular subtyping is now done by RNA expression profiling, which we'll cover on the next couple of slides. Treatment is multimodal, surgical resection, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy, with autologous stem cell transplant reserved for very high risk patients.

keypoints: Medulloblastoma arises in the cerebellum and can seed the leptomeninges
Staging requires whole spine MRI and lumbar puncture, thirty percent have spinal spread
High risk features include age under three, positive CSF cytology, and greater than one point five centimeters squared residual tumor
Treatment combines surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy, with transplant for very high risk disease
segments.voiceover: Key testable facts for medulloblastoma, it's a posterior fossa cerebellar tumor, thirty percent have leptomeningeal spread so you always image the whole spine and send CSF cytology. High risk disease means age under three, positive CSF cytology or spine MRI, more than one point five square centimeters of residual tumor, or large cell anaplastic histology. Treatment is surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy, with transplant reserved for the highest risk group.

This slide brings the four molecular subgroups of medulloblastoma to life using data pooled from seven series across four gene expression platforms. The age distribution panels at the top show that WNT tumors have a bimodal pattern peaking around age four to nine and again in the teens, SHH tumors are U shaped, most common in infants and then again in older adolescents and adults, Group 3 tumors cluster heavily in young children and decline with age, and Group 4 tumors peak broadly across childhood and adolescence. Overall, when you stratify the whole cohort by age, zero to three years accounts for about twenty one percent of cases, four to sixteen years is the bulk at sixty seven percent, and adults over seventeen make up twelve percent. The bottom row of survival curves is the real board takeaway, looking at all patients, WNT tumors have the best prognosis by far with survival near one hundred percent, Group 3 has the worst prognosis, and SHH and Group 4 fall in between. Notice the infant panel circled in the figure, Group 3 tumors in infants have a particularly poor outcome. This confirms that molecular subgrouping, not just histology, drives prognosis and increasingly treatment stratification in medulloblastoma.

keypoints: Four molecular subgroups, WNT, SHH, Group 3, and Group 4, each have distinct age distributions
WNT tumors carry the best prognosis, near one hundred percent survival
Group 3 tumors carry the worst prognosis, especially in infants
Molecular subgrouping predicts outcome independent of histology
segments.voiceover: For boards, memorize the prognosis ranking, WNT is best, close to one hundred percent survival, Group 3 is worst, particularly in infants, and SHH and Group 4 sit in between. This molecular classification is now a core part of medulloblastoma risk stratification.

This table is the detailed reference version of the four medulloblastoma molecular subgroups, and it's dense but very testable. WNT subgroup occurs in older children, adolescents, and adults, has an equal gender distribution, classic histology that's rarely large cell anaplastic, is rarely metastatic, and has a very good prognosis, driven by CTNNB1 mutations and WNT signaling activation. Sonic hedgehog, or SHH, subgroup occurs in young children as well as adolescents and adults, notably with a bimodal age pattern, equal gender distribution, desmoplastic nodular or classic histology, uncommon metastasis, and prognosis that's good in infants but intermediate in others, driven by mutations in PTCH1, PTCH2, SMO, or SUFU, plus GLI2 and MYCN amplification. Group 3 occurs in children and infants, is male predominant at a two to one ratio, has classic or large cell anaplastic histology, is very frequently metastatic, and has the poorest prognosis, characterized by isochromosome 17q and MYC amplification with very high MYC expression. Group 4 occurs across infants, children, and adults, is male predominant, has classic or large cell anaplastic histology, is frequently metastatic, with an intermediate prognosis, also showing isochromosome 17q plus CDK6 and MYCN amplification, but minimal MYC or MYCN expression compared to Group 3. The red underline on the prognosis row is your cue, that's the single row worth memorizing if you memorize nothing else on this slide.

keypoints: WNT, CTNNB1 mutation, very good prognosis, rarely metastatic
SHH, PTCH1, PTCH2, SMO, or SUFU mutations, good in infants, intermediate otherwise
Group 3, MYC amplification, male predominant, poorest prognosis, very frequent metastasis
Group 4, isochromosome 17q, CDK6 and MYCN amplification, intermediate prognosis
segments.voiceover: Boil this table down to genetics and prognosis. WNT means CTNNB1 mutation and excellent prognosis. SHH means PTCH, SMO, or SUFU mutations with an infant favorable pattern. Group 3 means MYC amplification and the worst prognosis with frequent metastasis. Group 4 means isochromosome 17q with CDK6 and MYCN amplification and an intermediate prognosis.

Retinoblastoma arises from photoreceptor elements in the inner retinal layer, and the classic presenting sign, shown in the photo here, is leukocoria, a white pupillary reflex often first noticed on a flash photograph, which is why parents frequently bring this up themselves. Diagnosis is confirmed by fundoscopic exam. Molecularly, retinoblastoma follows Knudson's two hit hypothesis, requiring biallelic loss of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene. About twenty five percent of cases are bilateral or multifocal and heritable, meaning the patient carries a germline RB1 mutation, while the remaining seventy five percent are unilateral and mostly nonhereditary, arising from two somatic hits in one eye. A high yield related entity is trilateral retinoblastoma, which is bilateral retinoblastoma plus a separate intracranial PNET, most commonly a pineoblastoma, with about a quarter of these intracranial tumors located in the suprasellar or parasellar region instead. Treatment follows the guiding philosophy of saving life while preserving useful vision whenever possible, using systemic chemotherapy, intra-ophthalmic artery chemotherapy for localized delivery, local therapies such as laser or cryotherapy, radiotherapy, and enucleation, surgical removal of the eye, reserved for advanced or refractory disease.

keypoints: Leukocoria, white pupillary reflex, is the classic presenting sign of retinoblastoma
Retinoblastoma requires biallelic loss of RB1, following the two hit hypothesis
Twenty five percent are bilateral and heritable, seventy five percent unilateral and nonhereditary
Trilateral retinoblastoma equals bilateral RB plus intracranial PNET, usually pineoblastoma
segments.voiceover: Remember retinoblastoma by its hallmark sign, leukocoria, and its genetics, biallelic RB1 loss following the two hit hypothesis, with bilateral disease being the heritable form. And know trilateral retinoblastoma, bilateral RB plus an intracranial PNET, most often a pineoblastoma.

This is the International Classification of Retinoblastoma, or ICRB, which fellows should know cold because it drives treatment choice. Group A is the smallest tumor, three millimeters or less. Group B is a larger tumor, or one located near the macula or the optic disc, or one with a small amount of clear subretinal fluid. Group C adds focal seeds, either subretinal or vitreous, still close to the tumor. Groups B and C together are sometimes remembered with the mnemonic SOAI, and these tumors, along with group A, are generally managed with systemic chemotherapy aimed at globe salvage. Group D means diffuse seeding, subretinal or vitreous seeds spread more than three millimeters from the tumor. Group E is extensive disease, occupying more than half the globe, with neovascular glaucoma, opaque media from hemorrhage, or invasion of the optic nerve, choroid, sclera, or anterior chamber. Group E eyes usually cannot be saved and go to enucleation.

keypoints: Group A, small tumor three millimeters or less
Groups B and C, larger or juxtapapillary tumor with focal seeds, treat with systemic chemotherapy
Group D, diffuse subretinal or vitreous seeding
Group E, extensive disease occupying over half the globe, needs enucleation
segments.voiceover: Remember it as a spectrum. Group A is tiny and easy. Groups B and C are bigger or awkwardly located but still salvageable with systemic chemotherapy, sometimes grouped together as SOAI. Group D means the seeding has spread diffusely. And Group E is the eye you cannot save, because of glaucoma, hemorrhage, or invasion beyond the retina, so it goes straight to enucleation.

This table is a high-yield summary for the differential diagnosis of an abdominal mass in a child. Wilms tumor peaks between two and five years old, arises in the kidney, and spreads to lung and liver. Hepatoblastoma peaks under two years old, arises in the liver, and spreads to the lungs. Desmoplastic small round cell tumor, or DSRCT, is different, it hits older kids and adolescents and young adults, can arise anywhere in the abdomen, and spreads along the peritoneum. Neuroblastoma peaks under five years old, arises from the adrenal gland or sympathetic chain, and spreads to bone marrow, liver, and skin. Rhabdomyosarcoma can occur at any age, arising from the prostate, uterus, bladder, or biliary tract, and spreads to lung, bone marrow, and lymph nodes. Ewing sarcoma, also any age, classically arises in the pelvis and spreads to lung and bone marrow. Lymphoma can arise anywhere in the abdomen at any age, spreading to bone marrow, skin, and CSF. And germ cell tumors, especially in adolescence, arise in the ovary, sacrum, or coccyx, spreading to lung, liver, and occasionally bone.

keypoints: Wilms tumor, kidney, peak age two to five, spreads to lung and liver
Hepatoblastoma, liver, peak under two, spreads to lungs
Neuroblastoma, adrenal or sympathetic chain, peak under five, spreads to bone marrow and liver
DSRCT and lymphoma can occur anywhere in the abdomen at any age
segments.voiceover: When you see an abdominal mass, let age and location narrow things down fast. Under five, think Wilms if it is kidney-based, neuroblastoma if it is adrenal or paraspinal, and hepatoblastoma if it is liver-based. In older children and adolescents, broaden your differential to rhabdomyosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, lymphoma, DSRCT, and germ cell tumors, since those can show up at any age.

This slide covers the genetics and classic presentation of Wilms tumor. On the genetic side, WT1 sits at chromosome eleven p one three and is associated with Denys-Drash syndrome and WAGR syndrome. WT2 sits at eleven p one five and is associated with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. TP53 mutations at seventeen p one three and FWT1 at seventeen q one two are also implicated in familial forms. On the clinical side, the classic presentation is a child brought in with a palpable abdominal mass, often found incidentally by a parent during bathing. Associated findings include hematuria, hypertension from renin secretion by the tumor, malaise, and fever. Fellows should recognize this constellation, a painless abdominal mass plus hypertension and hematuria in a toddler, as the textbook picture of Wilms tumor.

keypoints: WT1 at eleven p one three, linked to Denys-Drash and WAGR syndromes
WT2 at eleven p one five, linked to Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
Classic presentation, painless palpable abdominal mass in a toddler
Associated findings, hypertension, hematuria, malaise, fever
segments.voiceover: Two genes to anchor on, WT1 at eleven p thirteen tied to Denys-Drash and WAGR, and WT2 at eleven p fifteen tied to Beckwith-Wiedemann. Clinically, picture a toddler with an incidentally discovered abdominal mass, sometimes with hypertension from renin release and hematuria, that is your classic Wilms tumor vignette.

This is a dense summary table for Wilms tumor that fellows should memorize for boards. The primary site is almost always the kidney, and about eleven percent of cases are bilateral. Pathology shows the classic triphasic pattern, persistent blastema, dysplastic epithelial tubules, and supporting mesenchymal or stromal elements. The key genes are WT1 at eleven p one three and WT2 at eleven p fifteen point five. Prognostic factors include tumor stage, histology, where lack of anaplasia is favorable, age, where being younger than two years old with a small tumor under five hundred fifty grams and stage one favorable histology is a good sign, completeness of lung nodule response, and loss of heterozygosity at one p and sixteen q, which is unfavorable. Treatment involves nephrectomy, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy, and sometimes pre-operative chemotherapy is needed to shrink the tumor first. Two special treatment concerns to remember, never biopsy a stage one Wilms tumor because it can upgrade the stage, and radiotherapy should start within five to seven days after nephrectomy. Five-year overall survival is excellent, greater than ninety-five percent for stages one through three with favorable histology, and eighty-five percent overall.

keypoints: Kidney primary, eleven percent bilateral, classic triphasic histology
Key genes, WT1 at eleven p one three, WT2 at eleven p fifteen point five
Unfavorable factors, anaplasia and loss of heterozygosity at one p and sixteen q
Never biopsy stage one Wilms tumor, start radiotherapy within five to seven days post-nephrectomy
Five-year overall survival, greater than ninety-five percent for favorable stage one to three, eighty-five percent overall
segments.voiceover: Board pearls here, do not biopsy a suspected stage one Wilms tumor since that can upgrade its stage, and if radiotherapy is indicated it needs to start within five to seven days after nephrectomy. Favorable histology plus early stage carries an excellent prognosis, over ninety-five percent five-year survival, while anaplasia and loss of heterozygosity at one p and sixteen q push the tumor into an unfavorable category.

Two more Wilms tumor associations worth knowing for boards. First, WAGR syndrome, caused by a deletion at chromosome eleven p one three involving both the WT1 and PAX6 genes. The mnemonic spells it out, W for Wilms tumor, A for aniridia, absence of the iris, G for genitourinary malformations, which can include focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and renal failure, and R for mental retardation, or developmental delay. Second, stage five Wilms tumor, which is a distinct category referring to synchronous bilateral renal involvement at diagnosis, seen in about five percent of all Wilms tumor patients. Because both kidneys are involved from the start, these patients carry a substantially higher risk of end-stage renal disease, eleven to twenty percent compared to just zero point six percent in patients with unilateral disease.

keypoints: WAGR syndrome, Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary malformations, mental Retardation
Caused by chromosome eleven p one three deletion involving WT1 and PAX6
Stage five Wilms tumor means synchronous bilateral renal involvement at diagnosis
Stage five carries much higher end-stage renal disease risk, eleven to twenty percent
segments.voiceover: Two things to lock in. WAGR is your mnemonic, Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary malformations, and mental Retardation, from an eleven p thirteen deletion hitting WT1 and PAX6 together. And stage five Wilms tumor is not about size or spread, it specifically means both kidneys are involved at diagnosis, which is why these patients face a much steeper risk of ending up with end-stage renal disease.

This reference table lists the syndromes associated with Wilms tumor risk, and the four boxed at the top are the ones most likely to be tested. WAGR syndrome, from an eleven p one three deletion of WT1, presents with aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, and delayed-onset renal failure, and carries about a thirty percent Wilms tumor risk. Denys-Drash syndrome, from a point mutation in the zinc-finger region of WT1, also at eleven p one three, presents with ambiguous genitalia and diffuse mesangial sclerosis, and carries a very high risk, over ninety percent. Frasier syndrome, from a point mutation in the WT1 intron nine donor splice site, presents with ambiguous genitalia, streak gonads, and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, with a lower risk around eight percent. And Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, from dysregulation of imprinted genes including IGF2 and H19 at eleven p fifteen, presents with organomegaly, large birth weight, macroglossia, omphalocele, hemihypertrophy, ear pits and creases, and neonatal hypoglycemia, with about a five percent Wilms tumor risk. Further down the table are rarer associations, Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, mosaic variegated aneuploidy, Fanconi anemia D1, and several others, each with its own locus and estimated risk.

keypoints: WAGR, eleven p one three deletion of WT1, about thirty percent Wilms tumor risk
Denys-Drash, WT1 zinc-finger mutation, ambiguous genitalia, over ninety percent risk
Frasier syndrome, WT1 splice-site mutation, streak gonads, about eight percent risk
Beckwith-Wiedemann, eleven p fifteen, IGF2 and H19 dysregulation, about five percent risk
segments.voiceover: Four syndromes to distinguish by their WT1 or eleven p fifteen lesion. WAGR and Denys-Drash both hit WT1 at eleven p thirteen, but Denys-Drash carries a much higher Wilms tumor risk, over ninety percent, because it is a specific zinc-finger mutation rather than a deletion. Frasier syndrome is the milder cousin with a splice-site mutation and lower risk. And Beckwith-Wiedemann is the odd one out, driven by imprinted gene dysregulation at eleven p fifteen rather than WT1 itself, presenting with overgrowth features instead of genitourinary anomalies.

Now we move to neuroblastoma, the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood. It arises from neural crest cells of the sympathoadrenal lineage. Pathologically there is a maturation spectrum, from neuroblastoma, to ganglioneuroblastoma, to the fully mature and benign ganglioneuroma. Hereditary neuroblastoma is linked to mutations in PHOX2B and ALK. For workup, look for elevated urinary catecholamine metabolites, homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid, with VMA greater than seven milligrams per day being significant, along with functional imaging using F-eighteen FDOPA PET or I-one-two-three MIBG scan. Prognostic factors are numerous, staging system, which has evolved from the older Evans system, to INSS, to the current INRG system, age at diagnosis with a cutoff that has shifted from one year to one point five years, Shimada histology, degree of differentiation, MYCN amplification which predicts advanced disease and treatment failure, and chromosomal changes, where one p deletion, eleven q deletion, and seventeen q gain in a diploid tumor are unfavorable, while hyperdiploidy is more favorable. Treatment ranges widely by risk group, from observation alone in low-risk infants, to chemotherapy, surgery, radiotherapy, and thirteen-cis-retinoic acid, up to autologous stem cell transplant plus anti-GD2 immunotherapy for high-risk disease.

keypoints: Neural crest origin, maturation spectrum from neuroblastoma to ganglioneuroma
Hereditary neuroblastoma linked to PHOX2B and ALK mutations
Elevated urinary HVA and VMA, plus MIBG scan or FDOPA PET for workup
MYCN amplification and eleven q deletion predict advanced disease and worse outcome
High-risk treatment includes autologous stem cell transplant and anti-GD2 immunotherapy
segments.voiceover: Neuroblastoma spans a maturation spectrum from malignant neuroblastoma to benign ganglioneuroma. For workup, remember urinary HVA and VMA plus MIBG scan. For prognosis, MYCN amplification and eleven q deletion are the red flags for aggressive disease, while hyperdiploidy is reassuring. And for treatment, low risk may just need observation, but high-risk disease escalates all the way to autologous transplant combined with anti-GD2 immunotherapy.

This slide covers the clinical presentation of neuroblastoma, which can be dramatic because of its tendency to secrete catecholamines and metastasize early. Local symptoms depend on the primary site, an abdominal mass if it arises from the adrenal gland or paraspinal ganglia, or a chest mass if it arises in the posterior mediastinum, sometimes causing bone pain from local invasion. A paraspinal cervical or thoracic tumor can compress the sympathetic chain and cause Horner syndrome, remembered by the tetrad of myosis, or a constricted pupil, ptosis, or a droopy eyelid, enophthalmos, a sunken eye, and anhydrosis, or loss of sweating on that side of the face. Because most children present with metastatic disease at diagnosis, fellows should also recognize the systemic features, irritability, weight loss, bone pain from marrow or skeletal metastases, fever, proptosis, and periorbital ecchymoses, often called raccoon eyes, from metastasis to the orbital bones. Anemia is also common and is typically normochromic and normocytic, reflecting marrow infiltration.

keypoints: Local mass effect, abdominal or chest lump, depending on primary site
Horner syndrome, myosis, ptosis, enophthalmos, anhydrosis
Raccoon eyes, periorbital ecchymoses from orbital bone metastasis
Metastatic features, irritability, weight loss, bone pain, fever, proptosis
Normochromic normocytic anemia from marrow infiltration
segments.voiceover: Two exam findings are classic exam-question triggers. Horner syndrome, myosis, ptosis, enophthalmos, and anhydrosis, points to a cervical or thoracic paraspinal tumor compressing the sympathetic chain. And raccoon eyes, periorbital ecchymosis, points to metastatic disease infiltrating the orbital bones. Add in irritability, weight loss, bone pain, fever, and a normochromic normocytic anemia, and you have the classic picture of metastatic neuroblastoma at presentation.

This slide gives you the International Neuroblastoma Risk Group, or I N R G, staging system, which is the modern staging approach based on imaging rather than surgical findings. Stage L one is a locoregional tumor without image-defined risk factors, so it's surgically resectable up front. Stage L two is a locoregional tumor that does have one or more image-defined risk factors, meaning it's touching or encasing critical structures and isn't safely resectable initially. Stage M is distant metastatic disease, excluding the special M-S category. And M-S, the special stage, is an L one or L two tumor with metastatic disease confined only to skin, liver, and or bone marrow, without other distant spread. Below that, the slide reminds you of the classic Stage 4-S definition from the older I N S S system, which board exams still like to test, an infant under one year old with a localized primary tumor, stage one, two-A, or two-B, that has spread only to skin, liver, and or bone marrow, and critically the bone marrow involvement has to be minimal, less than ten percent of total nucleated cells, with negative MIBG or other imaging studies. This distinction matters because Stage 4-S, despite having metastatic disease, often has a favorable prognosis and can spontaneously regress.

keypoints: INRG L1: locoregional tumor, no image-defined risk factors
INRG L2: locoregional tumor with one or more image-defined risk factors
INRG M: distant metastatic disease (except MS)
INRG MS: L1/L2 tumor with mets confined to skin, liver, and/or marrow
INSS Stage 4S: age under 1, localized primary, marrow involvement under 10%
segments.voiceover: Know the four INRG stages, L one is locoregional without risk factors, L two is locoregional with image-defined risk factors, M is distant metastatic disease, and M-S is L one or L two with spread limited to skin, liver, or marrow. Separately, classic Stage 4-S requires age under one year, a localized primary tumor, and minimal marrow involvement under ten percent.

This dense table converts I N R G stage into a pre-treatment risk group, and it's built from just a handful of variables, M Y C N status, age, histology or grade of differentiation, eleven-q deletion, and ploidy. The big organizing principle is that M Y C N amplification trumps almost everything else. Look across the table and notice that any stage with M Y C N amplified, whether it's L one, L two, M, or M-S, lands in the high risk group regardless of age or histology, with the sole partial exception being M-S which the slide still flags separately. For M Y C N non-amplified, stage L one alone is always very low risk. For L two, the story depends on age and eleven-q deletion, patients under eighteen months without eleven-q deletion are low risk, but adding eleven-q deletion bumps them to intermediate, and for older patients, age over five with poorly differentiated or undifferentiated histology pushes them all the way to high risk even without amplification. For stage M, M Y C N non-amplified disease in infants under eighteen months is stratified by ploidy, hyperdiploid tumors are low risk while diploid tumors are intermediate risk, reflecting that hyperdiploidy is itself a favorable biological marker in young infants. Age eighteen months or older with M stage disease, non-amplified, is high risk. Finally M-S disease under eighteen months without eleven-q deletion is very low to low risk, but M Y C N amplified M-S disease is high risk. The exam-testable takeaways are that M Y C N amplification always means high risk, hyperdiploidy is protective specifically in infants with M stage disease, and eleven-q deletion upgrades risk within L two disease.

keypoints: MYCN amplification is high risk at essentially any stage
L1, MYCN non-amplified: always very low risk
L2: age under 18mo plus no 11q deletion is low risk; 11q deletion or age over 5 with poor differentiation raises risk
M stage, MYCN non-amplified, age under 18mo: hyperdiploid is low risk, diploid is intermediate risk
MS, MYCN amplified: high risk despite otherwise favorable stage
segments.voiceover: MYCN amplification pushes almost any stage into the high risk group. Among MYCN non-amplified L two disease, eleven-q deletion and older age with poor differentiation both raise risk. For M stage disease in infants under eighteen months, hyperdiploidy is low risk while diploidy is intermediate risk, since ploidy is a key favorable biology marker in young infants.

This is your summary card for hepatoblastoma, which is the most common liver tumor of childhood. The primary site is the liver itself, and the key special exam to remember is liver M R I for local staging. On risk factors, the board favorite is Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, but you should also know prematurity and low birth weight, familial adenomatous polyposis caused by A P C mutation, Aicardi syndrome, constitutional trisomy eighteen, Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome, glycogen storage disease, Sotos syndrome, and hemihyperplasia. These are all overgrowth or growth-dysregulation syndromes, which fits the biology of a tumor arising from immature liver progenitor cells. For poor prognosis factors, remember a higher PRETEXT score, meaning more extensive pretreatment disease, multifocal primary tumor, macrovascular involvement, portal vein involvement, extrahepatic tumor extension, tumor rupture, and metastasis, a low A F P level at diagnosis which is counterintuitive but true since very low A F P can indicate a more aggressive small cell undifferentiated histology, older age at diagnosis, and histology showing small cell undifferentiated pattern, which is unfavorable, as opposed to pure fetal histology, which is the good actor. Treatment is chemotherapy plus surgery, sometimes with checkpoint inhibitors under investigation, and liver transplantation for unresectable disease confined to the liver. Overall five-year survival exceeds sixty-five percent.

keypoints: Most common liver tumor in children; liver MRI for staging
Key risk factor: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, also FAP, trisomy 18, hemihyperplasia
Poor prognosis: high PRETEXT, multifocal, vascular invasion, rupture, metastasis
Low AFP and small cell undifferentiated histology are unfavorable; pure fetal histology is favorable
5-year overall survival over 65%
segments.voiceover: Hepatoblastoma is the most common pediatric liver tumor, linked to Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and other overgrowth conditions, staged with liver MRI. Poor prognosis factors include high PRETEXT score, vascular invasion, rupture, metastasis, low AFP, and small cell undifferentiated histology, while pure fetal histology is favorable. Overall five-year survival is over sixty-five percent.

This slide covers the Evans staging system for liver tumors, which is based on clinical evaluation by the surgeon and pathological findings at resection, in contrast to the imaging-based PRETEXT system you'll see next. Stage one is complete surgical resection with a margin free from tumor. Stage two is gross resection but with microscopic residual disease left behind. Stage three is gross resection with macroscopic residual disease, meaning visible tumor remains. And stage four is distant metastases. The diagrams below illustrate the Couinaud segmental anatomy of the liver, which underlies both the Evans system and the PRETEXT system, dividing the liver into the right posterior section, segments six and seven, the right anterior section, segments five and eight, the left medial section, segment four, and the left lateral section, segments two and three. Understanding these four sections is essential because PRETEXT staging, which we'll cover next, counts how many of these four contiguous sections are tumor-free rather than relying on surgical outcome, and that distinction, surgical staging versus radiographic staging, is a common board discrimination point.

keypoints: Evans staging is based on surgical and pathological findings, not imaging
Stage I: complete resection, margins tumor-free
Stage II: gross resection, microscopic residual disease
Stage III: gross resection, macroscopic residual disease
Stage IV: distant metastases; liver divided into 4 sections for staging
segments.voiceover: Evans staging is a post-surgical system, Stage one is complete resection with clear margins, Stage two has microscopic residual disease, Stage three has macroscopic residual disease, and Stage four is distant metastasis. The liver's four sections, right posterior, right anterior, left medial, and left lateral, form the anatomic basis for both Evans and PRETEXT staging.

Now we get to PRETEXT and POST-TEXT staging, which is the radiographic, pretreatment counterpart to the surgical Evans system, and it's the staging system actually used in most modern liver tumor protocols. Unlike Evans, PRETEXT is assigned before any treatment based on imaging alone, using those four liver sections from the previous slide, right posterior, right anterior, left medial, and left lateral. Stage one means three contiguous sections are tumor-free, so only one section is involved. Stage two means two contiguous sections are tumor-free, so two sections are involved. Stage three means only one contiguous section is tumor-free, so three sections are involved. And Stage four means no contiguous sections are tumor-free, meaning the tumor involves all four sections. POST-TEXT uses this same grading system but is reassessed after neoadjuvant chemotherapy to guide surgical planning. On top of the basic stage, any group can carry one or more annotation factors that flag additional risk, V for tumor ingrowth into the vena cava or all three hepatic veins, P for ingrowth into the portal vein or its bifurcation, E for extrahepatic contiguous tumor extension, F for multifocal tumor, R for tumor rupture at diagnosis, C for caudate lobe involvement, N for lymph node involvement, and M for distant metastasis. These annotation factors are what actually drive a lot of the poor prognosis features you saw on the hepatoblastoma summary slide.

keypoints: PRETEXT is imaging-based staging assigned before treatment; POST-TEXT reassesses after chemo
Stage I: 3 contiguous sections tumor-free (1 section involved)
Stage II: 2 sections tumor-free; Stage III: 1 section tumor-free; Stage IV: no tumor-free sections
Annotation factors: V (vena cava/hepatic veins), P (portal vein), E (extrahepatic), F (multifocal)
Additional annotations: R (rupture), C (caudate lobe), N (nodes), M (metastasis)
segments.voiceover: PRETEXT stages liver tumors by imaging before treatment, counting tumor-free liver sections out of four, Stage one has three tumor-free sections and Stage four has none tumor-free. POST-TEXT repeats this after chemotherapy. Annotation factors V, P, E, F, R, C, N, and M flag vena cava, portal vein, extrahepatic extension, multifocality, rupture, caudate involvement, nodal disease, and metastasis.

This table is a high-yield comparison of the three major pediatric and adolescent liver malignancies, hepatoblastoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, and the fibrolamellar variant of hepatocellular carcinoma, and the circled rows are the ones most likely to be tested. Age of presentation is a key discriminator, hepatoblastoma presents from birth to age three, hepatocellular carcinoma presents later, five to eighteen years, and fibrolamellar variant presents even later, ten to twenty years, often in adolescents and young adults without underlying liver disease.
