Associated congenital anomalies also separate them cleanly, hepatoblastoma is linked to dysmorphic features, hemihypertrophy, and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, hepatocellular carcinoma is linked to metabolic conditions like tyrosinemia or chronic hepatitis B, and fibrolamellar variant has no known associated anomalies, which is itself a distinguishing clue. A F P elevation follows a gradient, elevated in sixty to seventy percent of hepatoblastoma, fifty percent of conventional hepatocellular carcinoma, but only about ten percent of fibrolamellar variant, so a normal A F P in an adolescent liver mass should raise fibrolamellar variant on your differential rather than rule out malignancy. And the last circled row, abnormal vitamin B twelve binding protein, or transcobalamin, is essentially unique to fibrolamellar variant among these three, present in fibrolamellar but absent in the other two, making it a useful confirmatory marker when you're trying to distinguish fibrolamellar from conventional hepatocellular carcinoma.

keypoints: Age gradient: hepatoblastoma 0-3y, HCC 5-18y, fibrolamellar variant 10-20y
Associated anomalies: hepatoblastoma with Beckwith-Wiedemann/hemihypertrophy, HCC with metabolic disease, fibrolamellar with none
AFP elevated in 60-70% HB, 50% HCC, only about 10% fibrolamellar variant
Abnormal B12-binding protein (transcobalamin) is characteristic of fibrolamellar variant only
segments.voiceover: Use age to separate these three, hepatoblastoma under three years old, hepatocellular carcinoma five to eighteen, fibrolamellar variant ten to twenty. Hepatoblastoma links to Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, while fibrolamellar variant has no associated anomalies, low AFP elevation around ten percent, and a distinctive abnormal vitamin B twelve binding protein that the other two lack.

This slide summarizes malignant germ cell tumors, or MaGCT, which arise from primordial germ cells and can show up in a surprisingly wide range of locations. The most common primary sites are gonadal, the testes in boys or the ovaries in girls, but you also need to know the extragonadal sites, abdomen, mediastinum, the sacrococcygeal area, which is the classic site in infants, and intracranial, particularly the pineal and suprasellar regions. Pathologically these tumors span a spectrum, yolk sac tumor, mixed germ cell tumor, choriocarcinoma, and teratoma, which can be immature or mature. The key special exam is checking tumor markers, elevated beta-H C G and or A F P, and on the next slide you'll see exactly which marker goes with which histologic subtype. Treatment depends heavily on histology, primary site, and stage, but generally involves chemotherapy and surgery, with radiotherapy used selectively, and autologous stem cell transplant reserved as a salvage option for relapsed or refractory disease. The overall prognosis is genuinely reassuring, five-year survival varies with stage and histology but overall outcome is excellent, which is an important reassurance point for boards, since these tumors, despite sounding alarming, are among the more curable pediatric solid tumors.

keypoints: Most common sites: testes (boys), ovaries (girls); also sacrococcygeal, mediastinum, intracranial
Histologic spectrum: yolk sac tumor, mixed GCT, choriocarcinoma, mature/immature teratoma
Special exam: tumor markers, elevated beta-hCG and/or AFP
Treatment: chemotherapy plus surgery, selective radiotherapy, auto-HSCT for salvage
Overall 5-year survival is excellent
segments.voiceover: Malignant germ cell tumors most commonly arise in testes or ovaries, but also occur sacrococcygeally, mediastinally, and intracranially. Histology ranges from yolk sac tumor to choriocarcinoma to teratoma, and diagnosis leans on beta-hCG and AFP. Treatment is chemotherapy plus surgery with auto stem cell transplant reserved for salvage, and overall prognosis is excellent.

This table is the one you need to memorize cold for boards, because tumor markers are how you distinguish germ cell tumor subtypes without waiting for final pathology. Start with the terminology, seminoma is the term for the testicular tumor, dysgerminoma is the equivalent tumor in the ovary, and germinoma is the term used when this same histology arises at an extragonadal site. These are all low A F P and low beta-H C G, so a germ cell tumor with unremarkable or minimally elevated markers points you toward seminoma or dysgerminoma. Yolk sac tumor is the classic A F P producer, markedly elevated A F P with a negative beta-H C G, and this is the pattern to associate with infantile sacrococcygeal tumors and testicular tumors in young boys. Embryonal carcinoma flips that pattern, it's beta-H C G dominant with markedly elevated beta-H C G and only mildly elevated A F P. Choriocarcinoma is beta-H C G positive with a negative A F P, and remember it's most often found as one component within a mixed germ cell tumor rather than as a pure entity. Mature teratoma has both markers negative, which is one reason mature teratoma is considered benign, while immature teratoma can have a mildly elevated A F P in roughly a third of cases, reflecting immature yolk sac elements. Dermoid cyst, a form of mature teratoma, is also marker negative. Polyembryoma is positive for both markers. And mixed germ cell tumor, by definition containing more than one component, has marker levels that simply depend on which components are present, so you interpret the marker pattern based on what you know or suspect about the mixture.

keypoints: Seminoma/dysgerminoma/germinoma: low AFP, low beta-hCG
Yolk sac tumor: markedly elevated AFP, negative beta-hCG
Embryonal carcinoma: elevated beta-hCG, mildly elevated AFP
Choriocarcinoma: positive beta-hCG, negative AFP; usually a component of mixed GCT
Mature teratoma and dermoid cyst: both markers negative; immature teratoma may have mild AFP elevation
segments.voiceover: Memorize the marker pairs, yolk sac tumor means high AFP and negative beta-hCG, embryonal carcinoma means high beta-hCG with only mild AFP elevation, choriocarcinoma means positive beta-hCG with negative AFP, and mature teratoma or dermoid cyst are both markers negative. Seminoma, dysgerminoma, and germinoma are the same histology at different sites, all low marker tumors.

This table lines up the two classic pediatric bone sarcomas side by side, and it is a favorite way boards test you. Age helps separate them, Ewing sarcoma skews toward adolescents more than young children and is rare after age forty, while osteosarcoma peaks in adolescents and young adults and is rare under age five. Race is a clue too, Ewing sarcoma is notably rare in African and East Asian populations, while osteosarcoma shows no racial predilection. Predisposing factors are a big differentiator, Ewing sarcoma has no association with prior radiation and no known familial predisposition, whereas osteosarcoma is linked to radiation exposure and to cancer predisposition syndromes, specifically Li-Fraumeni syndrome from T P fifty-three mutations, and retinoblastoma. Ewing sarcoma classically causes constitutional symptoms like fever, while osteosarcoma usually does not. On imaging, Ewing sarcoma favors flat and long bones with a diaphyseal, shaft location and a laminated, onion-skin periosteal reaction, while osteosarcoma favors long bones, especially around the knee, in an epiphyseal or metaphyseal location, with a spiculated, sunburst pattern. Labs also diverge, Ewing sarcoma has a normal alkaline phosphatase but can show cytopenias if there's marrow involvement, while osteosarcoma classically raises alkaline phosphatase with a normal complete blood count. And histologically, Ewing sarcoma is a small round blue cell tumor driven by the E W S dash F L I one fusion, from a translocation between chromosome eleven band q twenty-four and chromosome twenty-two band q twelve, while osteosarcoma shows malignant spindle cells producing osteoid.

keypoints: Ewing sarcoma: diaphyseal, flat and long bones, onion-skin periosteal reaction, EWS-FLI1 fusion
Osteosarcoma: metaphyseal or epiphyseal, knee-predominant, sunburst periosteal reaction, elevated ALP
Osteosarcoma linked to Li-Fraumeni syndrome and retinoblastoma; Ewing has no known familial predisposition
Ewing sarcoma more often causes constitutional symptoms than osteosarcoma
Ewing sarcoma is rare in African and East Asian populations
segments.voiceover: Remember Ewing sarcoma as the diaphyseal, onion-skin, E W S dash F L I one tumor with constitutional symptoms and no familial link, versus osteosarcoma as the metaphyseal, sunburst, elevated alkaline phosphatase tumor tied to Li-Fraumeni and retinoblastoma predisposition.

This slide walks through the general treatment framework for bone sarcoma, which applies to both Ewing sarcoma and osteosarcoma with some key differences. Treatment starts with preoperative, or neoadjuvant, chemotherapy to shrink the tumor before surgery. Surgery follows, and limb-sparing resection is now possible in about ninety percent of cases, sparing patients from amputation. A critical step at surgery is assessing the histopathologic response to that preoperative chemotherapy, meaning how much viable tumor remains, because this response grade is one of the strongest predictors of outcome and can guide whether postoperative chemotherapy needs to be intensified. After surgery, postoperative chemotherapy continues to eliminate micrometastatic disease. Radiation therapy is where the two tumor types really diverge, radiation is used for Ewing sarcoma in specific situations, large tumors, pelvic primaries, and cases with close surgical margins, because Ewing sarcoma is fairly radiosensitive. Osteosarcoma, on the other hand, is relatively radiation-resistant, so radiation plays essentially no role in its management, and local control depends almost entirely on complete surgical resection.

keypoints: Sequence: neoadjuvant chemo, then surgery, then adjuvant chemo
Limb-sparing surgery achievable in about 90% of cases
Histopathologic response to preop chemo predicts prognosis
Radiation used for Ewing sarcoma with large, pelvic, or close-margin tumors
Osteosarcoma is relatively radioresistant, so surgery drives local control
segments.voiceover: Both bone sarcomas follow neoadjuvant chemo, surgery, then adjuvant chemo, with limb-sparing surgery possible in ninety percent of cases. The key exam point is radiation, it helps in Ewing sarcoma for large, pelvic, or close-margin tumors, but osteosarcoma is relatively radioresistant, so complete surgical resection is essential there.

This slide lists the factors that predict a poor prognosis in osteosarcoma, and these show up frequently on boards as the features that should raise your concern for a worse outcome. The single most important one is detectable metastatic disease at diagnosis, and the lung is by far the most common site of metastasis in osteosarcoma, so a baseline chest CT is essential at diagnosis. Larger primary tumor size is also unfavorable, bigger tumors carry more risk. Axial skeletal primaries, meaning tumors of the spine, pelvis, or skull rather than the extremities, tend to do worse, partly because they're harder to resect completely. Similarly, a proximal location within the limb, closer to the trunk, carries worse prognosis than a distal one, again largely because achieving a wide surgical margin is more difficult. Incomplete resection, meaning positive or close margins after surgery, is a major adverse factor since local control is critical in a radioresistant tumor. And finally, a poor histologic response to preoperative chemotherapy, meaning a high percentage of viable tumor remaining at the time of surgery, predicts a higher risk of relapse and worse survival.

keypoints: Detectable metastatic disease at diagnosis, most commonly to lung, is the strongest adverse factor
Larger tumor size worsens prognosis
Axial skeletal or proximal limb primaries are harder to resect and carry worse outcomes
Incomplete surgical resection is a major adverse prognostic factor
Poor histologic response to preoperative chemotherapy predicts higher relapse risk
segments.voiceover: For osteosarcoma prognosis, remember metastatic disease at diagnosis, especially to lung, larger tumor size, axial or proximal primaries, incomplete resection, and poor histologic response to preoperative chemo as the key adverse factors.

This slide summarizes rhabdomyosarcoma, the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood. Primary sites are distributed across the body, with head and neck accounting for the largest share at about forty percent, followed by the genitourinary tract at around twenty percent, extremities at about twenty percent, and the retroperitoneal region contributing roughly ten percent, trunk sites making up the rest. Pathology and genetics distinguish the two major subtypes. Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma is the unfavorable subtype, driven by a translocation between chromosome two band q thirty-five and chromosome thirteen band q fourteen, and less commonly between chromosome one band q thirty-six and chromosome thirteen band q fourteen, translocations that fuse PAX transcription factor genes to FOXO1. Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, the more favorable subtype, is instead characterized by loss of heterozygosity at the eleven p fifteen locus. A cluster of features defines unfavorable risk, advanced pretreatment stage, gross residual disease left after surgery, tumors larger than five centimeters, metastatic disease at diagnosis, alveolar histology itself, an unfavorable primary site, and age older than nine years, since older children have a higher incidence of both advanced disease and alveolar histology. Treatment is multimodal, combining chemotherapy, surgery, and radiotherapy.

keypoints: Most common sites: head and neck, then genitourinary tract and extremities
Alveolar RMS (unfavorable): t(2;13)(q35;q14) or rarely t(1;13)(q36;q14)
Embryonal RMS (favorable): loss of heterozygosity at 11p15
Unfavorable factors: advanced stage, residual disease, tumor over 5 cm, metastasis, alveolar histology, age over 9
Treatment is multimodal: chemotherapy, surgery, and radiotherapy
segments.voiceover: Rhabdomyosarcoma splits into alveolar, the unfavorable subtype with a two thirteen translocation, and embryonal, the favorable subtype with eleven p fifteen loss of heterozygosity. Unfavorable features include advanced stage, residual disease, large tumor size, metastasis, and age over nine, and treatment combines chemotherapy, surgery, and radiotherapy.

This slide continues the rhabdomyosarcoma discussion by defining favorable versus unfavorable primary tumor sites, which is one of the key inputs into risk stratification alongside stage, histology, and resectability. Favorable sites include the orbit, the head and neck excluding parameningeal locations, the genitourinary tract excluding the bladder and prostate, and the biliary tract. These sites tend to be more accessible for complete resection or respond well to combined therapy, and they carry a better prognosis. Unfavorable sites include the bladder and prostate, the extremities, cranial parameningeal locations, meaning sites near the skull base and meninges where local extension into the central nervous system is a real risk, and a catch-all other category that includes the trunk and retroperitoneum. Recognizing which bucket a given primary site falls into is essential for boards, because site is one of the factors used directly in risk group assignment and treatment intensity.

keypoints: Favorable sites: orbit, head and neck excluding parameningeal, nonbladder/nonprostate genitourinary tract, biliary tract
Unfavorable sites: bladder and prostate, extremity, cranial parameningeal, trunk and retroperitoneum
Cranial parameningeal sites carry risk of direct CNS extension
Primary site is a key input into RMS risk stratification
segments.voiceover: For RMS, favorable sites are orbit, nonparameningeal head and neck, nonbladder nonprostate genitourinary tract, and biliary tract. Unfavorable sites are bladder and prostate, extremity, cranial parameningeal, and trunk or retroperitoneum, and site feeds directly into risk stratification.

This slide is a rapid-fire summary of when radiation therapy is used across the major pediatric hematology and oncology diagnoses, and it's a great one to memorize as a quick reference table for boards. For A L L, radiation is used for total body irradiation as part of stem cell transplant conditioning, and for local relapses or infiltration, especially testicular relapse. For non-Hodgkin lymphoma, radiation is reserved for acute tumor compression, like airway compromise, or for refractory tumors, it is not routine. For Hodgkin disease, radiation is combined with chemotherapy as low-dose involved field radiation, especially in high-risk or relapsed patients. CNS tumors usually require radiation, particularly high-grade gliomas, medulloblastoma in children older than three years, where radiation can be safely given, and germ cell tumors. Neuroblastoma uses radiation for high-risk disease and for spinal cord compression as an emergency. Wilms tumor gets postoperative radiation briefly directed at the tumor bed when there's intraoperative tumor spill, or for inoperable disease. Retinoblastoma usually requires radiation, and chemotherapy is often used first specifically to delay radiation until the child is at least one year old, to protect facial bone growth. Hepatoblastoma radiation is not curative but can shrink unresectable disease or minimal residual disease. Osteosarcoma has no role for radiation since it's relatively radioresistant. Ewing sarcoma uses radiation when residual disease is suspected after surgery. And rhabdomyosarcoma is moderately radiosensitive, using higher doses especially in intermediate and high-risk disease, within dose limits to protect normal tissue.

keypoints: ALL: TBI for transplant conditioning, plus local relapse such as testicular disease
CNS tumors and retinoblastoma usually require radiation; RB chemo often delays RT until age 1
Neuroblastoma and Wilms tumor: radiation for high-risk disease, spinal cord compression, or tumor spill

segments.voiceover: Key radiosensitive tumors are CNS tumors, retinoblastoma, and Hodgkin disease, which usually need radiation, while osteosarcoma never does. Ewing sarcoma and rhabdomyosarcoma are moderately radiosensitive, and neuroblastoma, Wilms tumor, and A L L use radiation mainly for high-risk disease or emergencies like cord compression or spill.
